title: A repeatable opening description
body:
Begin with the involved bone and longitudinal and cross-sectional location. Then give density, margin or zone of transition, cortical changes, and ancillary findings such as matrix and periosteal reaction. This sequence makes your assessment useful even when you cannot name the lesion confidently.

ACR connection: This 2023 ACR consensus system evaluates a potentially neoplastic bone lesion on diagnostic radiographs, combines imaging findings with pertinent cancer history, and links the resulting risk category to management. It addresses risk first; morphology, patient age, symptoms, and clinical context then support a focused differential.

ACR connection: Practice this sequence: age and symptoms/cancer history; exact bone, number, and epicenter; lucent/sclerotic/mixed density and matrix; full margin and host response; cortex, fracture risk, and soft tissues; succinct risk assessment and focused differential; then the next imaging or specialist step. This is an author-created synthesis of the article, useful for visual cases and follow-up questions.
prompt: How would you organize the first sentence and subsequent description of an unfamiliar bone lesion?
answer: Locate it, describe its density and border, assess cortex and remodeling, then characterize matrix and periosteal reaction before offering a focused differential.

title: Lucent, sclerotic, and mixed describe appearance
body:
A lucent lesion attenuates less than surrounding bone. A dense lesion may reflect actual sclerosis, calcified matrix, or periosteal bone; these are different processes. When possible, specify a lucent lesion with chondroid mineralization instead of collapsing all increased density into the word sclerotic.

ACR connection: Density chiefly guides differential diagnosis rather than directly establishing malignancy. Lytic lesions include benign tumors, primary malignancy, myeloma, metastasis, infection, and metabolic disease. A diaphyseal medullary lesion may become apparent through cortical scalloping because there are fewer internal trabeculae to outline marrow destruction than in the ends of a long bone.
prompt: Why can calling a heavily calcified chondrosarcoma sclerotic be misleading?
answer: Its density may come from mineralized chondroid matrix within a destructive lucent lesion rather than production of sclerotic bone.

title: Shaft lucency can imply cortical loss
body: In a tubular-bone shaft, cancellous bone contributes relatively little to radiographic attenuation. A visible lucency there often implies loss of at least part of a cortex, even if that cortex is seen en face. Compare orthogonal views rather than assuming the lesion is purely medullary.
prompt: A shaft lesion looks intramedullary on one projection. What should you check next?
answer: Inspect the orthogonal view for cortical involvement; an en face cortical lesion can masquerade as a medullary lucency.

title: End-of-bone lucency behaves differently
body: At the ends of long bones and in nontubular bones, cancellous bone contributes much more to attenuation. A medullary lesion can therefore be radiographically lucent without full-thickness cortical loss. Do not apply the shaft-lucency inference indiscriminately to the calcaneus or epiphysis.
prompt: Does a lucent calcaneal lesion necessarily require cortical destruction?
answer: No. Replacing or destroying cancellous bone can produce substantial lucency in a nontubular bone with a relatively thin cortex.

title: Draw the transition in your mind
body: The zone of transition is the interface between a predominantly lucent lesion and normal bone. A narrow interface is sharply traceable; a wide interface blends into the adjacent bone. Use it to estimate behavior rather than merely as a decorative adjective in the report.
prompt: What makes a zone of transition wide?
answer: You cannot confidently trace a sharp boundary between the lucent lesion and normal bone; the margin is indistinct or nongeographic.

title: IA: geographic with a sclerotic rim
body: A geographic lesion with a definite sclerotic rim has a narrow transition and usually reflects slow growth that allowed a host-bone response. This is a strongly reassuring pattern, although a descriptor never replaces the full imaging and clinical context.
prompt: What does a geographic lucency with a complete sclerotic border imply about growth?
answer: Typically slow, nonaggressive behavior; it is the Lodwick IA pattern and is strongly associated with benign processes.

title: IB: sharp does not guarantee benignity
body: A geographic lesion with a sharp but nonsclerotic margin is Lodwick IB. Many such lesions are benign, including some enchondromas and giant cell tumors, but metastases and myeloma can also look geographic. A narrow transition alone cannot clear an older patient's lesion.
prompt: Which malignant processes can have a well-defined nonsclerotic border?
answer: Metastasis and plasma-cell lesions can; a geographic IB margin narrows behavior without proving benign histology.

title: IC: geographic yet aggressive
body: A lesion may remain roughly geographic while its boundary becomes poorly defined. This Lodwick IC pattern has a wide transition and reflects more aggressive growth. The differential includes malignant tumors but also locally aggressive giant cell tumor and Langerhans cell histiocytosis.
prompt: Can a lesion be geographic and still have a wide zone of transition?
answer: Yes. An ill-defined geographic border is Lodwick IC and should be treated as an aggressive pattern.

title: Moth-eaten versus permeative
body: Moth-eaten destruction has relatively larger discrete holes; permeative destruction has tiny channels that may be very subtle. Both are nongeographic aggressive patterns with substantially overlapping differentials. In a case presentation, recognizing their aggressive nature matters more than forcing an exact distinction.
prompt: What are the principal broad categories for a permeative lesion?
answer: Aggressive neoplasm, including round-cell and plasma-cell tumors, and infection; neither the pattern nor the tiny holes are specific for malignancy.

title: Aggressive describes behavior
body:
A wide transition, cortical destruction, or aggressive periosteal response indicates rapid or destructive behavior. Infection and some nonmalignant tumors can produce these findings. Conversely, a malignant lesion may initially have relatively bland margins. State the behavior and the likely cause as separate judgments.

ACR connection: Margins, periosteal response, erosion, fracture, extra-osseous extension, and cancer history drive risk scoring. Density, matrix, and site help predict histology. A cartilage matrix can occur in benign or malignant lesions; an aggressive reaction can occur in infection. During oral cases, first describe what you see, then explain risk, then use discriminators to narrow the differential.
prompt: Does an aggressive radiographic appearance establish a sarcoma?
answer: No. Infection, LCH, and locally aggressive nonmalignant tumors can overlap; an indeterminate aggressive lesion usually needs further evaluation and often tissue diagnosis.

title: Use radiographs or CT for the transition
body: Apply the zone-of-transition concept to radiographs and CT, and to lytic or predominantly lytic lesions. MRI can show a sharply demarcated malignant tumor because its contrast separates marrow and tumor well. A neat MRI edge must not overrule destructive radiographic findings.
prompt: Why is a sharp T2 MRI margin insufficient evidence that a lesion is benign?
answer: The radiographic zone-of-transition rule is not valid on MRI; highly aggressive malignancies may be sharply delineated there.

title: Scalloping is a pattern, not a diagnosis
body: Endosteal scalloping is erosion of the inner cortical surface by a medullary process. It occurs in enchondroma and fibrous dysplasia, but also in plasmacytoma and chondrosarcoma. Describe its depth and extent, then interpret it in the specific lesion rather than equating scalloping with malignancy.
prompt: Name both benign and malignant causes of endosteal scalloping.
answer: Enchondroma and fibrous dysplasia are benign examples; chondrosarcoma and plasmacytoma are malignant examples.

title: Cortical breakthrough and extraosseous extension
body: Full-thickness destruction or permeation permits a lesion to reach the surrounding soft tissues. This is concerning but still overlaps infection and locally aggressive lesions. A substantial soft-tissue component may be invisible on radiographs, especially in the pelvis, so assess cross-sectional imaging when indicated.
prompt: Does absence of a visible radiographic soft-tissue mass exclude extraosseous disease?
answer: No. Cross-sectional imaging is more sensitive, and substantial tumor may escape radiographic detection, particularly in the pelvis.

title: Expansion alone is not a benign certificate
body:
Expansile remodeling means bone growth has widened the involved segment. It occurs in benign lesions, locally aggressive GCT, and some metastases. Marked cortical attenuation can suggest more aggressive remodeling, but the preserved-versus-thinned distinction is imperfect and must be combined with margins and other features.

ACR connection: Slow growth permits concurrent endosteal resorption and periosteal apposition, replacing native cortex with a neocortex. Uniform growth yields a smooth thin shell; varying growth produces ridges, septations, or lobulation; a thick shell indicates enough time for dense new bone formation. In Fig. 2, identify smooth, ridged/septated, and lobulated examples.
prompt: Can a renal or lung metastasis expand bone rather than simply destroy it?
answer: Yes. Malignant lesions can remodel expansilely; expansion by itself does not distinguish them from benign cystic or chondroid lesions.

title: Fracture occurs in benign and malignant lesions
body:
A lesion can weaken bone through cortical destruction or remodeling until trivial trauma produces fracture. The presence of fracture establishes structural failure, not histologic grade. A fractured simple bone cyst, NOF, or enchondroma can become painful and develop periosteal reaction that was absent before fracture.

ACR connection: An actual pathological fracture adds 2 points. Benign lesions can fracture, but pathological fractures are especially consequential in malignant disease: pain, loss of function, worse outcomes, and possible contamination of adjacent tissues. In the Fig. 10 metastasis example, fracture converts a 5-point geographic ill-defined lesion into a 7-point high-risk lesion.
prompt: What does a pathologic fracture tell you, and what does it not tell you?
answer: It shows weakened bone and structural risk; it does not by itself separate benign from malignant disease.

title: Periosteal reaction is a host response
body:
Periosteal new bone can follow tumor, infection, fracture, or metabolic disturbance. Its architecture reflects the tempo and continuity of irritation. Describe the pattern, examine the underlying lesion, and search for a fracture rather than treating any periosteal reaction as a tumor diagnosis.

ACR connection: Radiographic periosteal new bone typically takes about 10 days to 3 weeks after a stimulus to become visible, sometimes sooner in younger patients. Solid reaction suggests a slower process, whereas interrupted or complex reaction suggests a faster process. Osteomyelitis and other nonmalignant processes can nevertheless produce aggressive appearances; describe indolent versus aggressive rather than equating reaction with benign versus malignant.
prompt: What common nonneoplastic processes can produce periosteal reaction?
answer: Fracture, infection, and metabolic disorders can; benign tumors can also irritate the periosteum.
overlap: This principle appears in both the textbook/exhibit and the ACR paper; reviewed together here.

title: Solid reaction suggests time to mature
body:
A thin or thick solid periosteal reaction generally indicates a slower process that allowed new bone to consolidate. Osteoid osteoma, stress injury, and chronic infection are examples. A mature response describes the response itself, so a coexisting fracture must still be considered when the lesion looks malignant.

ACR connection: When native cortex is retained, slowly added layers of periosteal bone can form a dense solid reaction. Fig. 3a illustrates this appearance. Separate that surface response from the neocortex of a remodeled expansile lesion. A smooth solid response helps judge tempo, while diagnosis still depends on the lesion and clinical context.
prompt: What does thick, consolidated periosteal new bone usually suggest?
answer: A slower or sustained irritation, often nonaggressive; examples include osteoid osteoma and chronic infection, while fracture-related reaction may accompany any underlying lesion.
overlap: This principle appears in both the textbook/exhibit and the ACR paper; reviewed together here.

title: Thin linear reaction can flag an occult fracture
body: A single thin line of periosteal new bone often reflects recent irritation, particularly healing fracture in children. When it appears around an otherwise indolent lesion such as fibrous dysplasia or a simple bone cyst, look for an occult pathologic fracture; maturation over subsequent weeks supports healing.
prompt: New thin linear periosteal reaction surrounds a previously quiet cyst. What is a useful explanation?
answer: An occult or healing pathologic fracture; the line may later consolidate into solid new bone.

title: Lamellated reaction is aggressive but nonspecific
body:
Multiple periosteal layers create an onion-skin appearance. It is a classic association with Ewing sarcoma, but infection and LCH can produce a similar response. Combine the reaction with lesion location, age, cortical destruction, and a soft-tissue mass to build the differential.

ACR connection: Lamellated or onion-skin periosteal reaction reflects repeated layers of new bone. The article discusses it in Ewing sarcoma and other small round blue cell tumors, but also in Langerhans cell histiocytosis and osteomyelitis. Fig. 3c demonstrates the pattern; corrected Fig. 9 shows why a sclerotic margin plus lamellated reaction can still warrant biopsy.
prompt: Is an onion-skin periosteal reaction diagnostic of Ewing sarcoma?
answer: No. It supports aggressive irritation but also occurs with infection and occasionally LCH.
overlap: This principle appears in both the textbook/exhibit and the ACR paper; reviewed together here.

title: Perpendicular spicules signal aggressive irritation
body:
Perpendicular new bone is often described as hair-on-end when relatively parallel and sunburst when divergent. Both imply an aggressive process; splitting those labels usually contributes less than identifying the underlying lesion and its matrix. Metastasis can produce this pattern as well as primary sarcoma.

ACR connection: Parallel spicules create a hair-on-end appearance, frequently associated with malignant lesions such as osteosarcoma. Divergent spicules create a sunburst pattern; the article describes contributions from periosteal response and mineralized tumor matrix. Inspect Fig. 4 and say whether the spicules are parallel or divergent instead of using an imprecise aggressive label alone.
prompt: Must a sunburst or hair-on-end reaction come from osteosarcoma?
answer: No. It is an aggressive reaction pattern that can occur with other tumors, including metastases.
overlap: This principle appears in both the textbook/exhibit and the ACR paper; reviewed together here.

title: A Codman triangle describes interrupted reaction
body:
When rapid lesion growth disrupts the periosteal new bone behind its advancing edge, the remaining elevated periosteum can form a triangle. This supports aggressive behavior in an intraosseous lesion, but it is not a specific histologic diagnosis and the surface-lesion caveat still applies.

ACR connection: A Codman angle is elevated, abruptly interrupted periosteum at the shoulder of a mass that has lifted and broken through it. Fig. 3b illustrates the relationship. Mixed patterns in Fig. 5 combine divergent spicules with Codman angles or lamellation with parallel spicules, indicating variable growth and sometimes transformation in a pre-existing lesion.
prompt: What does a Codman triangle represent mechanistically?
answer: Interrupted periosteal new bone at a rapidly advancing process; interpret it with the origin and other features of the lesion.
overlap: This principle appears in both the textbook/exhibit and the ACR paper; reviewed together here.

title: No periosteal response does not reassure by itself
body: Myeloma characteristically lacks a periosteal response, and many metastases show none. A lesion with no periostitis can therefore be either benign or malignant. It is more useful to ask whether the observed response fits the suspected entity than to use absence as a blanket exclusion of cancer.
prompt: Which important malignancies often lack periosteal reaction?
answer: Multiple myeloma and many metastases; absence of reaction cannot establish benignity.

title: A malignant lesion can have benign fracture callus
body: A nonaggressive periosteal pattern generally favors an indolent intraosseous process, but healing of a pathologic fracture through a malignant lesion can produce mature or linear periosteal bone. If lesion destruction and periosteal response seem discordant, inspect carefully for a fracture.
prompt: How can osteosarcoma coexist with a seemingly benign periosteal reaction?
answer: A fracture through the tumor can provoke ordinary reparative periosteal new bone; the underlying destructive lesion still requires assessment.

title: Do not grade a surface lesion by the same rule
body: The usual aggressive-versus-nonaggressive periosteal patterns were developed for lesions growing inside bone. A benign periosteal chondroma can generate productive bone at its edge that appears interrupted or perpendicular. Establish whether the process is intraosseous or on the surface before applying the pattern rule.
prompt: Why can apparent interrupted new bone beside a periosteal chondroma be misleading?
answer: It is a surface lesion with peripheral host-bone production; the intraosseous periosteal-reaction behavior rule does not directly apply.

title: Recognize rings, arcs, and flocculent cartilage
body: Mineralized chondroid matrix forms small rings and arcs. When abundant, these coalesce into a popcorn or flocculent appearance. This identifies a cartilage-producing family, while symptoms, skeletal site, cortical behavior, and extraosseous extension determine how concerning that chondroid lesion is.
prompt: Does identifying rings-and-arcs mineralization establish an enchondroma?
answer: No. It identifies chondroid matrix, which occurs in benign and malignant cartilage lesions.

title: Cloudlike mineralization suggests osteoid
body: Osteoid matrix has a fluffy, amorphous, cloudlike appearance rather than discrete chondroid rings. In an aggressive metaphyseal lesion in a child or young adult, this strongly supports osteosarcoma. Some osteosarcomas lack a conspicuously mineralized matrix, so absence does not exclude the diagnosis.
prompt: What matrix appearance most strongly supports conventional osteosarcoma on radiographs?
answer: Ill-defined cloudlike or fluffy osteoid mineralization in an aggressive lesion, interpreted with age and location.

title: Ground glass reflects woven bone
body: The hazy ground-glass appearance associated with fibrous dysplasia reflects immature woven bone within a fibrous lesion. It can approximate bone density without showing normal trabecular architecture. Look for a long central lesion, mild expansion, and a nonaggressive overall appearance rather than relying on density alone.
prompt: What produces the ground-glass density of fibrous dysplasia?
answer: Woven immature bone; the term fibrous matrix is a convenient imaging label rather than a literal claim that soft fibrous tissue is mineralized.

title: Use the physis as a longitudinal landmark
body:
In children, specify epiphysis, metaphysis, metadiaphysis, or diaphysis and whether the lesion crosses a growth plate. An epiphyseal epicenter has a more restricted differential than a huge lesion that merely reaches the end of the bone. Distinguish origin from extent.

ACR connection: State the exact bone and whether the epicenter is epiphyseal, metaphyseal, or diaphyseal. Metaphyseal processes often relate to turnover or vascularity; diaphyseal lesions include marrow-based tumors such as Ewing sarcoma and lymphoma. An apophysis is an epiphyseal equivalent. An adolescent apophyseal abnormality may represent avulsion when the imaging and history fit. These are diagnostic tendencies, not exclusion rules.
prompt: Why is a very large tumor reaching an epiphysis not automatically an end-of-bone tumor?
answer: Its epicenter may be metaphyseal or diaphyseal; extension to the joint does not establish epiphyseal origin.
overlap: This principle appears in both the textbook/exhibit and the ACR paper; reviewed together here.

title: Central, eccentric, cortical, or surface
body:
Describe the lesion's cross-sectional epicenter. Some lesions are central within or fill the medullary cavity; others are eccentric, intracortical, or external to the bone. NOF can extend inward enough to blur the cortical-versus-eccentric distinction, so avoid false precision when the anatomy is genuinely overlapping.

ACR connection: Describe a lesion as central intramedullary, eccentric intramedullary, intracortical, or surface based. This may be obscured by a large destructive tumor, but it is highly useful when preserved. An intracortical lucency with surrounding cortical thickening in an adolescent with salicylate-responsive pain supports osteoid osteoma.
prompt: How would you describe a cortical-origin NOF that extends deeply into the medullary cavity?
answer: A cortical or eccentric endosteal lesion with medullary extension; acknowledge the overlap rather than forcing an artificial distinction.
overlap: This principle appears in both the textbook/exhibit and the ACR paper; reviewed together here.

title: Remember epiphyseal equivalents
body: The patella, tarsals, and apophyseal sites share parts of the epiphyseal lesion differential; the chapter also illustrates carpal involvement in chondroblastoma. A lesion in one of these bones should prompt the same age-and-location reasoning used for epiphyseal lesions in long bones.
prompt: What does an epiphyseal-equivalent location add to a young patient's lytic-lesion differential?
answer: It makes chondroblastoma an important consideration even when the lesion is in a tarsal bone, patella, or apophysis rather than a long-bone epiphysis.

title: Keep the end-of-bone differential focused
body: Chondroblastoma and GCT are the principal tumor considerations at the end of a long bone, separated mainly by skeletal maturity and border. In older patients consider metastasis. Geodes are important mimics; clear cell chondrosarcoma and an epiphyseal brown tumor are much less common possibilities.
prompt: What is a concise differential for a true epiphyseal or subarticular lesion?
answer: Chondroblastoma, GCT, and age-appropriate metastasis, with geode as a key mimic; rare alternatives include clear cell chondrosarcoma and brown tumor.

title: Age trims a differential without making disease impossible
body: The chapter uses under-30 and over-40 rules as practical discriminators: chondroblastoma, ABC, and LCH favor the younger group; myeloma, metastasis, and chondrosarcoma rise in older adults. These are strong prioritization tools with acknowledged exceptions, not biological impossibility thresholds.
prompt: How should you use the chapter's age cutoffs during an oral case?
answer: Prioritize plausible entities for the age, then combine with imaging and history; do not label rare exceptions impossible or let a long differential obscure a necessary biopsy.

title: The sacral primary-tumor triad
body: A focused primary sacral tumor differential includes chordoma, chondrosarcoma, and GCT. GCT tends to be eccentric, lacks matrix calcification, and is less strikingly T2 bright than chordoma or chondrosarcoma. These are comparative clues, not a substitute for imaging the full lesion.
prompt: An eccentric sacral lytic mass has no calcification and modest T2 signal. Which primary sacral tumor rises?
answer: GCT rises relative to the often central chordoma and the markedly T2-bright, sometimes calcified chordoma or chondrosarcoma.

title: Posterior spinal elements have a short core list
body: ABC, osteoblastoma, osteoid osteoma, and fibrous dysplasia are core posterior-element considerations. In an expansile lesion in a child or adolescent, ABC and osteoblastoma deserve particular attention. Calcification, nidus size, MRI fluid levels, and the response to NSAIDs help refine the list.
prompt: What should you consider for an expansile posterior-element lesion in an adolescent?
answer: ABC and osteoblastoma, with fibrous dysplasia and osteoid osteoma depending on matrix, size, and symptoms.

title: A small lesion can cause a large inflammatory response
body: Osteoid osteoma, osteoblastoma, chondroblastoma, LCH, and infection form the chapter's bone-irritator group. Marrow edema, periostitis, synovitis, and pain may be much more conspicuous than the lesion. Track the center of the reaction back to the actual nidus or focus.
prompt: What core entities belong in the bone-irritator group?
answer: Osteoid osteoma, osteoblastoma, chondroblastoma, LCH, and infection.

title: Fluid-fluid levels identify layering, not a specific tumor
body: ABC commonly has blood-fluid levels, but the same finding can appear in GCT, chondroblastoma, osteoblastoma, and telangiectatic osteosarcoma. Correlate with radiographs and look for solid nodular enhancement; otherwise an aggressive tumor may be mislabeled as a benign cyst.
prompt: Name four tumors that can show ABC-like fluid-fluid levels.
answer: GCT, chondroblastoma, osteoblastoma, and telangiectatic osteosarcoma.

title: Ask whether the lesion actually explains pain
body: NOF, simple bone cyst, enchondroma, and fibrous dysplasia are often incidental. Fracture can make a benign lesion hurt, and shoulder pain beside a chondroid lesion may come from tendinopathy, bursitis, or arthritis. Attribute symptoms carefully before turning pain into a malignancy label.
prompt: A humeral enchondroma is found during shoulder MRI for pain. What must be resolved?
answer: Whether pain localizes to the lesion or has a separate mechanical explanation, and whether fracture or concerning lesion features are present.

title: MRI defines extent rather than radiographic behavior
body: For a suspected malignant bone tumor, MRI assesses marrow and soft-tissue extent, epiphyseal invasion, and separate tumor foci within the same bone. It complements the radiographic pattern. A well-defined MRI boundary cannot undo a wide radiographic transition or cortical destruction.
prompt: What does MRI add once radiographs suggest osteosarcoma?
answer: Local staging: intramedullary extent, extraosseous component, epiphyseal involvement, and skip lesions in the same bone.

title: A lytic tumor may remain nonspecific
body:
Without a characteristic mineralized matrix, an aggressive lesion may not be specifically identifiable on imaging. A useful interpretation can still describe aggressiveness, give a concise age-and-site differential, identify mimics, and explain why further evaluation is required. Guessing an exotic name adds little.

ACR connection: Many fibrous, cystic, lipomatous, and vascular lesions lack a recognizable mineralized matrix; myeloma and many metastases also appear purely lucent. Fibrous dysplasia may show ground-glass density, a peripheral rind, or mixed density from its fibrous and osseous components. Intraosseous lipoma can contain dystrophic calcification from fat necrosis, and hemangioma can show thickened trabeculae.
prompt: If an aggressive lytic lesion has no matrix, what can you still accomplish?
answer: Describe its behavior and extent, prioritize a focused differential, seek a recognizable mimic, and guide appropriate further evaluation rather than forcing a specific histologic diagnosis.
