title: Multiplicity changes the question
body:
Multiple lesions can redirect the differential toward metastases, myeloma, LCH in children, polyostotic fibrous dysplasia, enchondromatosis, or metabolic disease. Distribution matters: juxta-articular bone islands differ from diffuse blastic deposits, and ipsilateral polyostotic FD differs from a random metastatic distribution.

ACR connection: Multiple lesions increase concern for metastases, myeloma, or lymphoma, but can also reflect benign polyostotic processes such as enchondromatosis, fibrous dysplasia, and Langerhans cell histiocytosis. State the observed distribution and seek appropriate wider assessment when indicated; do not assume that a local radiograph proves a lesion is solitary.
prompt: What extra information should you give after saying multiple bone lesions?
answer: Their density, morphology, age context, and distribution, including axial versus appendicular, juxta-articular clustering, and unilateral or segmental involvement.
overlap: This principle appears in both the textbook/exhibit and the ACR paper; reviewed together here.

title: GCT: four features to seek together
body: For a long-bone GCT, seek skeletal maturity, an epiphyseal lesion reaching the subarticular bone, eccentricity unless the lesion fills the cross-section, and a geographic predominantly nonsclerotic margin. These are the chapter's strong discriminators; they should support a coherent diagnosis rather than be used as exception-free laws.
prompt: A subarticular distal-radius lesion has a nonsclerotic border. What other features strengthen GCT?
answer: Closed physes, an eccentric medullary epicenter or full-width involvement, and a geographic rather than permeative destruction pattern.

title: GCT can be locally destructive
body: GCT can expand markedly, thin or destroy cortex, fracture, and develop fluid-fluid levels. A more rapidly growing lesion may have an ill-defined geographic margin. Its locally aggressive behavior can resemble malignancy, but a moth-eaten or permeative pattern should prompt reconsideration of the diagnosis.
prompt: Would major expansion or a pathologic fracture exclude GCT?
answer: No. Both occur in locally aggressive GCT; assess whether the subarticular location, maturity, and geographic pattern still fit.

title: GCT favors particular long-bone ends
body: Common sites include the knee region and proximal femur, with a distinctive predilection for the distal radius. Most patients are skeletally mature, often young or middle-aged adults, although older adults can be affected. In an older patient, history and multiplicity may instead favor metastasis.
prompt: What lesion should rise for an eccentric distal-radius epiphyseal lucency in a skeletally mature adult?
answer: GCT, especially if it reaches the articular surface and has a geographic nonsclerotic margin; age and cancer history still matter.

title: Know why GCT treatment is anatomically sensitive
body: The chapter describes resection for GCT, with selected use of monoclonal-antibody treatment to arrest growth and promote a reparative bony shell before less radical surgery. Preserving the adjacent joint can be difficult. GCT is classed as locally aggressive despite occasional pulmonary spread; management belongs with the treating tumor team.
prompt: Why might GCT therapy aim to create a bony shell before surgery?
answer: To make curettage or a less radical operation more feasible near an articular surface, particularly at anatomically difficult sites such as the distal radius.

title: Chondroblastoma: young and epiphyseal
body: Chondroblastoma strongly favors an open or recently closed physis and an epiphyseal or epiphyseal-equivalent epicenter. It is usually a round geographic lucency, often with a sclerotic margin. Metaphyseal extension across a closing physis is compatible with an epiphyseal origin.
prompt: How do you separate typical chondroblastoma from typical GCT at the end of a long bone?
answer: Chondroblastoma favors open or recently closed physes and often a sclerotic margin; GCT strongly favors mature physes and a predominantly nonsclerotic geographic margin.

title: Chondroblastoma often irritates bone and joint
body: Chondroblastoma commonly causes extensive marrow edema and adjacent synovitis, explaining why it is often symptomatic rather than incidental. MRI may show fluid-fluid levels from ABC-like change. Neither marked edema nor fluid levels should displace the age-and-epiphyseal-location clues.
prompt: Why can a small chondroblastoma produce conspicuous pain and MRI abnormalities?
answer: It is a bone irritator that can provoke marrow edema and synovitis; secondary cystic hemorrhagic change can add fluid-fluid levels.

title: Absent calcification does not exclude chondroblastoma
body: Only approximately 40%-60% of chondroblastomas show mineralization in the chapter's discussion. Do not require visible chondroid calcification before diagnosing the pattern. A sclerotic epiphyseal lesion in the proximal humerus, proximal femur, distal femur, or an equivalent site still needs maturity and morphology assessment.
prompt: A young patient's epiphyseal lucency lacks calcification. Is chondroblastoma excluded?
answer: No. Calcification is variable and absent in roughly half of cases; location, maturity, border, and associated edema are more useful.

title: Enchondroma has different small- and large-bone faces
body: In larger bones, medullary chondroid mineralization may be the only radiographic clue to enchondroma. In phalanges, it commonly appears as an expansile geographic lucency without visible matrix. The lesion can be central or eccentric and may scallop the endosteum.
prompt: Why is an unmineralized lucent phalangeal lesion still compatible with enchondroma?
answer: Enchondromas in the hands and feet often lack visible chondroid mineralization and may expand the bone or present after fracture.

title: Describe low-grade chondroid uncertainty honestly
body: In a medullary cartilage lesion lacking aggressive findings, wording such as a low-grade chondroid lesion can express the overlap between enchondroma and low-grade chondrosarcoma. Tiny asymptomatic classic lesions are more straightforward. Symptoms and suspicious structural features should trigger a more cautious assessment, not canned reassurance.
prompt: Why may low-grade chondroid lesion be more accurate wording than a definitive enchondroma label?
answer: Imaging and even core histology can overlap with low-grade chondrosarcoma; the description should preserve that uncertainty when relevant.

title: Do not overlook the cartilage-lesion warning features
body: The chapter highlights attributable pain, size greater than 5 cm, deep scalloping exceeding two-thirds of cortical thickness, and epiphyseal centering as reasons to consider low-grade chondrosarcoma and orthopedic evaluation. These are risk clues rather than isolated proof; cortical destruction and a soft-tissue component are more concerning still.
prompt: Which features make a presumed enchondroma less comfortably routine?
answer: Attributable pain, size over 5 cm, deep endosteal scalloping, epiphyseal centering, periosteal reaction, cortical destruction, or extraosseous tumor.

title: Ollier and Maffucci are not interchangeable
body: Ollier disease denotes multiple enchondromas. Maffucci syndrome adds soft-tissue vascular malformations, which can contain phleboliths. Both syndromic settings increase concern for malignant transformation. Rounded soft-tissue phleboliths are distinct from the rings-and-arcs cartilage matrix inside bone.
prompt: Multiple enchondromas coexist with soft-tissue phleboliths. What syndrome should you name?
answer: Maffucci syndrome; enchondromatosis without the associated vascular malformations is Ollier disease.

title: Osteochondroma requires corticomedullary continuity
body: An osteochondroma is a cartilage-capped osseous outgrowth whose cortex and marrow continue into the parent bone. It may be pedunculated or broad-based and sessile. An osseous excrescence without this relationship is an exostosis, but cannot automatically be called an osteochondroma.
prompt: What is the key imaging relationship that distinguishes osteochondroma from a generic exostosis?
answer: Continuity of both cortex and medullary cavity with the parent bone.

title: Explain why an osteochondroma points away from the joint
body: The lesion originates from growth-plate cartilage displaced at the physeal edge and is usually metaphyseal or metadiaphyseal. With longitudinal growth, its orientation tends to point away from the parent physis. Symptoms can result from bursitis, nerve impingement, fracture, or the palpable mass rather than malignancy.
prompt: What benign mechanisms can make an osteochondroma painful?
answer: Adventitial bursitis, nerve impingement, or fracture, in addition to local mass effect; pain requires evaluation but is not automatically transformation.

title: Assess the cartilage cap and hereditary setting
body: The cartilage cap is normally thin after skeletal maturity. The chapter uses a cap thicker than 2 cm on MRI as a major warning for transformation, interpreted with maturity and context. Flat-bone lesions and multiple hereditary exostoses carry greater concern; MHE also causes metaphyseal undertubulation around the knees.
prompt: What findings raise concern for chondrosarcoma arising in an osteochondroma?
answer: A thick cartilage cap, particularly over 2 cm after maturity, and a concerning growing mass; flat-bone origin and MHE strengthen the concern.

title: Fibrous dysplasia: integrate several familiar appearances
body: FD commonly affects ribs, pelvis, long bones, and craniofacial bones. It can look lucent, ground glass, sclerotic, or remodeled, especially after years of evolution. A central metadiaphyseal or diaphyseal lesion with a nonaggressive margin and mild expansion is a useful recurring pattern.
prompt: What combination supports FD more than a single ground-glass descriptor?
answer: Typical distribution, a long central lesion, mild remodeling or scalloping, and an overall nonaggressive appearance with little or no periosteal response.

title: FD can bend and expand a long bone
body: A long FD lesion may fill the medullary cross-section and cause mild expansion, endosteal scalloping, or bowing. Extensive proximal-femoral involvement can produce varus angulation, the shepherd's-crook deformity. When the lesion does not fill the cavity, a sclerotic border is often evident.
prompt: What proximal-femoral deformity is associated with extensive FD?
answer: A shepherd's-crook varus deformity caused by chronic remodeling of the involved proximal femur.

title: Polyostotic FD has a patterned distribution
body: Polyostotic FD often involves one extremity and the ipsilateral hemipelvis rather than a random scatter. The chapter contrasts generally stable postpubertal monostotic disease with polyostotic disease that may continue to grow in adulthood. McCune-Albright syndrome combines polyostotic FD, cafe-au-lait pigmentation, and endocrine abnormalities.
prompt: What are the three elements of McCune-Albright syndrome described here?
answer: Polyostotic fibrous dysplasia, cafe-au-lait skin pigmentation, and endocrine abnormalities such as precocious puberty.

title: FD may be scintigraphically active while indolent
body: FD can show substantial Tc-99m MDP uptake despite a nonaggressive radiographic appearance. It generally lacks periosteal reaction unless complicated by a fracture. New focal pain or reaction should therefore prompt a search for a complication and careful reassessment rather than assuming the tracer activity is cancer.
prompt: Does marked bone-scan uptake by an FD lesion prove aggressive behavior?
answer: No. FD can be avid; interpret uptake with morphology and look for fracture or other explanation if new pain or periosteal reaction is present.

title: Recognize the usual NOF without an expansive differential
body: NOF is common in children and favors the metaphysis or metadiaphysis near the knee and distal tibia. It originates in or abuts cortex, with a sharply defined usually sclerotic rim. Larger lesions can be lobulated or soap-bubbly yet retain a classic nonaggressive pattern.
prompt: What features make a pediatric cortical lucency a classic NOF?
answer: A lower-limb metaphyseal or metadiaphyseal site, cortical or eccentric endosteal location, geographic border, and usually a sclerotic rim.

title: NOF symptoms usually reflect a complication
body: NOF is generally asymptomatic unless a large lesion develops a stress or pathologic fracture. Corresponding periosteal reaction should lead you to inspect for fracture. With maturity, lesions often fill from their periphery with bone and become small endosteal sclerotic streaks, so adult residual sclerosis can represent a healed lesion.
prompt: How can an NOF change after skeletal maturity without becoming malignant?
answer: It often involutes by ossifying from the periphery inward, leaving inconspicuous endosteal sclerosis.

title: Separate NOF terminology from osteofibrous dysplasia
body: Fibrous cortical defect and NOF are histologically the same lesion; some use a 2 cm size cutoff for the names. Osteofibrous dysplasia is a different process favoring the anterior tibial cortex in children, often with multiple foci. Do not merge these similarly named entities.
prompt: What location should suggest osteofibrous dysplasia rather than an ordinary NOF?
answer: A lesion centered in the anterior tibial cortex in a child, particularly when multifocal along that cortex.

title: Simple bone cyst strongly favors a central epicenter
body: Simple bone cyst is a fluid-containing lesion that usually begins near the physis and grows toward the shaft. It strongly favors children and young adults and a central medullary location. The proximal humerus and proximal femur account for most cases; an eccentric epicenter should make you reconsider.
prompt: What two features are particularly helpful for a simple bone cyst?
answer: A central medullary location and a young patient, usually under 30; the proximal humerus or femur is especially typical.

title: A dependent fallen fragment is a strong cyst clue
body: Simple bone cyst often becomes symptomatic when it fractures. A small detached cortical fragment can sink dependently within the fluid cavity, creating the fallen-fragment sign. This is highly characteristic in the correct setting and is more useful than a generic description of an expansile lucency.
prompt: Why does a small dependent bone fragment favor a simple bone cyst?
answer: The fragment can settle within a fluid-filled cavity after fracture, producing the characteristic fallen-fragment sign.

title: MRI can clarify a radiographically ambiguous cyst
body: A simple cyst may resemble FD on radiographs; MRI can establish its fluid nature. Typical cysts are not primary epiphyseal lesions, although extension into the epiphysis after physeal closure can occur. Multiple internal locules are possible, so the older term unicameral can be misleading.
prompt: Why should an epiphyseal epicenter make you question a simple bone cyst?
answer: Typical cysts start near the physis and extend into the shaft, rather than originating in the epiphysis; uncommon postclosure extension is a different issue.

title: The calcaneal cyst, lipoma, and pseudocyst share a neighborhood
body: A simple bone cyst can have a triangular appearance in the anteroinferior calcaneus. A similar lesion with central mineralization may represent an intraosseous lipoma. A normal trabecular pseudocyst can occupy the same region but tends to lack a true sharply bounded lesion; cross-sectional imaging can resolve uncertainty.
prompt: How can a calcaneal lucency be refined beyond bone cyst?
answer: Assess whether it is a true bounded lesion, whether central calcification or fat supports lipoma, and whether indistinct normal trabecular architecture supports pseudocyst.

title: ABC typically expands a young patient's bone
body: ABC usually occurs in children and young adults and is characteristically expansile, often eccentric and metaphyseal, with a geographic margin. Pelvis and spinal posterior elements are additional sites. The age-under-30 and expansion rules are strong practical clues, while rare earlier nonexpansile presentations are acknowledged.
prompt: What radiographic and demographic pattern most supports ABC?
answer: An expansile geographic eccentric lesion in a young person, commonly metaphyseal or in the posterior spinal elements.

title: ABC-like change can occur inside another tumor
body: Use ABC for the primary lesion and ABC-like change for hemorrhagic cystic change within another tumor. GCT, chondroblastoma, osteoblastoma, and telangiectatic osteosarcoma can all show it. The cystic appearance must not obscure a solid underlying neoplasm with a different treatment pathway.
prompt: What is the distinction between ABC and ABC-like change?
answer: ABC is the primary lesion; ABC-like change describes similar fluid-level-containing hemorrhagic spaces within another tumor.

title: Search for nodular solid enhancement
body: An ABC may be dominated by fluid-fluid levels, but discrete solid nodular enhancement should prompt concern for an underlying tumor rather than a simple ABC diagnosis. Correlate the entire lesion with the radiographic aggression; telangiectatic osteosarcoma is the critical mimic because management differs substantially.
prompt: What imaging finding should interrupt a reflex diagnosis of ABC on MRI?
answer: Nodular solid postcontrast enhancement, especially with aggressive radiographic margins or periosteal reaction, suggests another tumor with ABC-like change.

title: Osteoid osteoma: find a small nidus
body: OO is usually a cortical lesion with a lucent nidus smaller than 2 cm, sometimes centrally mineralized, and surrounding dense reactive bone. Long bones and spinal sites are typical. The nidus may be difficult to see on radiographs or MRI; CT is particularly useful when the surrounding reaction dominates.
prompt: What is the best targeted imaging step when marked focal edema suggests OO but no nidus is visible?
answer: CT to identify the small lucent nidus and any central mineralization, using the edema pattern to localize the search.

title: OO can present as synovitis rather than dramatic cortical thickening
body: OO is often painful, classically worse at night and relieved by NSAIDs. An intra-articular focus can produce synovitis instead of the usual prominent periosteal response. Nocturnal pain is not specific: chronic osteomyelitis can also hurt at night and resemble OO.
prompt: Does nocturnal pain by itself distinguish OO from Brodie abscess?
answer: No. Both can cause night pain and reactive sclerosis; a demonstrable small nidus and the complete clinical and imaging picture are needed.

title: OO ablation follows precise lesion localization
body: The chapter describes percutaneous ablation, sometimes with concurrent biopsy, for symptomatic OO. Accurate nidus localization is essential because extensive edema can draw attention away from the small target. The source emphasizes that this is a very painful procedure requiring appropriate anesthesia and procedural planning.
prompt: Why must the target be the nidus rather than simply the region of marrow edema?
answer: The nidus is the actual tumor; edema is a much larger reactive phenomenon and can misdirect localization.

title: Osteoblastoma overlaps OO but is larger
body: Osteoblastoma is histologically related to OO but typically has a focus larger than 2 cm and often occurs in the second or third decade. It can look like a large OO or an expansile soap-bubble lesion with ABC-like change. Pain generally responds less well to NSAIDs than OO pain.
prompt: How do size and symptoms help distinguish osteoblastoma from OO?
answer: Osteoblastoma is typically larger than 2 cm and its pain is usually less NSAID-responsive; both can cause substantial reactive edema and periosteal bone.

title: Posterior-element osteoblastoma can contain stippled matrix
body: Approximately half of osteoblastomas in the chapter occur in spinal posterior elements, where stippled mineralization is common. An expansile posterior-element lesion with edema, calcification, and possible fluid levels should therefore not be called ABC solely because of its cystic component.
prompt: An expansile adolescent posterior-element lesion has small calcifications and fluid levels. What alternative to ABC matters?
answer: Osteoblastoma with ABC-like change; its posterior-element predilection and possible stippled mineralization are useful clues.

title: Vertebral hemangioma: trabeculae and fat
body: A typical vertebral hemangioma has thickened vertically oriented trabeculae, creating a corduroy or celery-stalk appearance on sagittal imaging. Many contain abundant fat, which helps account for low CT attenuation and high signal on fat-bright MRI sequences. Describe a classic benign pattern without overreacting to the word lesion.
prompt: What two structural components help recognize a typical vertebral hemangioma?
answer: Coarse vertical trabeculae and abundant intralesional fat.

title: Brown tumor requires a hyperparathyroid context
body: Brown tumors are lytic reparative lesions from excessive osteoclastic activity and hemorrhage. They may expand and can be multiple, but their morphology is nonspecific. Seek accompanying hyperparathyroid bone disease: radial middle-phalangeal subperiosteal resorption, distal-clavicular or sacroiliac subchondral resorption, and the clinical biochemical context.
prompt: What finding makes brown tumor a meaningful differential rather than a generic mnemonic entry?
answer: Other evidence of hyperparathyroidism, especially characteristic subperiosteal resorption in the fingers; the lesion itself is not specific.

title: Conventional osteosarcoma: young, metaphyseal, and aggressive
body: An aggressive metaphyseal lesion in a child or young adult should place conventional osteosarcoma high on the list, particularly with osteoid mineralization. Most are mixed lytic and blastic, but predominantly lytic or densely sclerotic forms occur. A geographic ill-defined margin is possible; destruction need not always be maximally permeative.
prompt: What classic combination strongly suggests conventional osteosarcoma?
answer: Young age, metaphyseal location, aggressive destruction and periosteal reaction, with cloudlike osteoid matrix when visible.

title: Use the whole osteosarcoma pattern
body: Perpendicular or interrupted periosteal reaction commonly accompanies osteosarcoma. These findings support aggressive behavior but are shared with other tumors and infection. Conversely, a tumor with little mineralized matrix can look nonspecific; do not require every classic feature before considering osteosarcoma.
prompt: What should you avoid when an aggressive young patient's lesion lacks visible osteoid?
answer: Do not exclude osteosarcoma solely because matrix is absent; correlate site, age, cortical destruction, reaction, and MRI findings.

title: A physis is not a reliable tumor barrier
body: MRI staging of osteosarcoma evaluates the soft-tissue component, marrow extent, crossing into the epiphysis, and skip lesions elsewhere in the same bone. Describe these as anatomic questions for the case discussion. A sharply defined MRI margin does not downgrade the tumor's radiographic aggressiveness.
prompt: What are the important local-staging questions after recognizing osteosarcoma?
answer: How far it extends in marrow and soft tissue, whether it crosses into the epiphysis, and whether separate same-bone skip foci are present.

title: Telangiectatic osteosarcoma can masquerade as ABC
body: A fluid-level-filled lesion may be telangiectatic osteosarcoma even when little osteoid is visible. Aggressive radiographic margins, concerning periosteal reaction, and enhancing solid nodules argue against a straightforward ABC. Both imaging and sampled tissue may overemphasize the hemorrhagic component, so communicate the suspicious areas.
prompt: Which combination makes ABC an unsafe sole diagnosis?
answer: Fluid-fluid levels plus aggressive radiographs and solid nodular enhancement; these should raise telangiectatic osteosarcoma or another underlying neoplasm.

title: Parosteal osteosarcoma is a surface tumor
body: Parosteal osteosarcoma grows outside the bone in intimate contact with cortex, most often near the posterior distal femur. It is frequently densely mineralized and may have little medullary invasion. It lacks the normal cortex-and-marrow architecture expected within an osteochondroma despite its bone-like density.
prompt: How is parosteal osteosarcoma distinguished from an osteochondroma structurally?
answer: It is a dense surface mass lacking normal corticomedullary architecture and continuity through the lesion, rather than a true cartilage-capped outgrowth of normal-appearing parent bone.

title: Central maturation helps distinguish parosteal tumor from MO
body: When a parosteal osteosarcoma is not completely mineralized, its densest mineralization tends to be central. Myositis ossificans matures at the periphery. The chapter describes better prognosis than conventional osteosarcoma, especially without medullary invasion, but it still requires oncologic evaluation rather than being dismissed as mature bone.
prompt: What mineralization distribution favors myositis ossificans over parosteal osteosarcoma?
answer: Peripheral circumferential maturation favors MO; central-dominant dense mineralization is more concerning for the surface osteosarcoma pattern.

title: Ewing favors young patients and an aggressive permeative pattern
body: Ewing commonly involves long-bone diaphysis or metadiaphysis in the first two decades; pelvis, ribs, and scapula can be involved in the second or third decade. Permeative cortical destruction and aggressive lamellated, interrupted, or perpendicular reaction are typical, although radiographic destruction can be surprisingly subtle.
prompt: What age-location-pattern combination should suggest Ewing sarcoma?
answer: A young patient with a diaphyseal or metadiaphyseal permeative lesion, or a flat-bone lesion, often with aggressive periosteal response and a large soft-tissue mass.

title: A large mass with modest bone findings is a warning
body: Ewing can permeate cortex through many tiny channels and form an extraosseous mass disproportionate to the apparent radiographic destruction. Lymphoma is a key alternative. Ewing does not characteristically produce lesional matrix, although reactive sclerosis in spared bone may create a mixed-density impression.
prompt: A large soft-tissue mass accompanies barely visible permeative bone change. Which tumors should be prominent?
answer: Ewing sarcoma and lymphoma; subtle radiographic cortical change does not imply a small or indolent lesion.

title: Bone lymphoma may resemble Ewing
body: Lymphoma may cause permeative or radiographically occult cortical destruction and a large associated soft-tissue component. Periosteal reaction can be subtle or absent, but when present may be aggressive. Judge the entire marrow, cortical, and soft-tissue pattern, recognizing that a relatively inconspicuous radiograph can underestimate extent.
prompt: What imaging pattern brings lymphoma alongside Ewing in the differential?
answer: An aggressive or subtle permeative marrow-cortical process with a disproportionately large extraosseous component, with or without aggressive periosteal response.

title: Lymphoma can be sclerotic too
body: Although permeative lysis is an important pattern, reactive sclerosis can occur in lymphoma. An ivory vertebra is one possible presentation, so lymphoma is not confined to a purely lucent differential. Interpret focal sclerosis with distribution, architecture, clinical context, and potential mimics such as Paget disease.
prompt: Can an ivory vertebra be caused by lymphoma?
answer: Yes. Lymphoma can produce marked reactive sclerosis, including an ivory vertebra, despite its common destructive presentations.

title: Myeloma has more than one radiographic face
body: Myeloma may produce multiple small punched-out lucencies, a diffuse moth-eaten pattern, scattered discrete lesions, or generalized osteopenia without a conspicuous focal lesion. It favors axial marrow and proximal appendicular skeleton. Multiple vertebral compression fractures in an appropriate middle-aged or older patient should raise concern.
prompt: Does myeloma require multiple obvious punched-out skull lesions?
answer: No. It may present with diffuse osteopenia, vertebral compression fractures, or less discrete destructive change.

title: Myeloma often lacks reparative bone
body: Untreated myeloma lesions classically lack a sclerotic rim and periosteal new bone, reflecting a predominantly osteolytic process. Pathologic fractures are common. The age-over-40 rule is a practical prioritization tool; it should not be turned into an absolute exclusion in a younger patient with compelling findings.
prompt: What absence of host-bone reaction supports a plasma-cell lesion?
answer: A purely lytic pattern without a sclerotic rim or appreciable periosteal response, especially in an appropriate older patient.

title: Radiographs and bone scans can underestimate myeloma
body: Myeloma burden is often greater on cross-sectional imaging than radiographs suggest. Bone scintigraphy can also underrepresent disease and may even be normal. In a case discussion, do not allow a negative bone scan to override convincing lytic disease; state the modality limitation without treating one named advanced test as universally mandated.
prompt: Why does a negative conventional bone scan fail to exclude extensive myeloma?
answer: Myeloma can produce predominantly lytic disease with little corresponding osteoblastic tracer response, so scintigraphy may underestimate its extent.

title: Plasmacytoma is a solitary plasma-cell presentation
body: The chapter reserves plasmacytoma for a solitary osseous plasma-cell neoplasm without the systemic marrow involvement of myeloma. It is generally lytic, may be large and expansile, can extend into soft tissue, and can have geographic or aggressive margins. Imaging resemblance alone does not establish that it is truly solitary.
prompt: What additional distinction is needed before calling a lesion solitary plasmacytoma?
answer: The clinical and systemic evaluation must distinguish a solitary plasma-cell lesion from systemic myeloma; imaging of one mass alone cannot make that distinction.

title: Metastasis belongs in many adult differentials
body: Metastases can be purely lytic, mixed, or blastic and can have geographic or permeative borders. Periosteal reaction is variable and often absent. In adults over 40, consider metastasis whenever a lesion lacks confidently benign features, while avoiding an automatic cancer label for a recognizable benign mimic.
prompt: Does a geographic margin or lack of periosteal reaction exclude metastasis?
answer: No. Either can occur; age, known primary, distribution, and lesion-specific features must guide the assessment.

title: Primary-tumor clues are suggestive, not definitive
body: Multiple blastic lesions commonly suggest prostate cancer in a male or breast cancer in a female, but other primaries overlap. Renal cell carcinoma characteristically produces large lytic deposits and sometimes few bulky lesions. These patterns help prioritize history and evaluation, but imaging often cannot identify the primary with certainty.
prompt: What primary is especially associated with a bulky lytic metastasis rather than a blastic pattern?
answer: Renal cell carcinoma; however, primary-site inference remains probabilistic and requires clinical correlation.

title: Aggressive cartilage in an adult raises chondrosarcoma
body: An aggressively destructive lesion with mineralized chondroid matrix in an older adult strongly suggests chondrosarcoma. Without mineralization it may be indistinguishable from other aggressive lytic tumors. The chapter favors an over-40 population but acknowledges younger patients, including transformation of a pre-existing cartilage lesion.
prompt: How does visible chondroid matrix improve an aggressive-lesion differential?
answer: It identifies a cartilage-producing malignancy pattern, making chondrosarcoma prominent in the appropriate adult setting; absent matrix leaves a less specific aggressive differential.

title: Cartilage risk depends on site and structural change
body: A pelvic medullary chondroid lesion deserves substantially more concern than a similar phalangeal lesion. New cortical destruction, extraosseous chondroid matrix, or periosteal reaction raises concern for more aggressive disease. A core sample can miss the highest-grade region, so correlate pathology with the most suspicious imaging component.
prompt: Why should a benign-sounding core result not automatically settle a destructive chondroid lesion?
answer: Cartilage grading overlaps and sampling can underestimate grade; the imaging-pathology mismatch needs discussion, especially with cortical breakthrough or a soft-tissue mass.

title: Myositis ossificans matures from outside inward
body: MO produces circumferential peripheral ossification around a less mineralized center. CT can establish this zonal maturation when a radiograph is ambiguous. The contrast with the central-dominant mineralization of a surface osteosarcoma is a key visual distinction; a remembered trauma history alone is not sufficient to decide between them.
prompt: Which is more useful than a trauma history when separating MO from a mineralized surface tumor?
answer: The distribution of mineralization: peripheral circumferential maturation supports MO, whereas a centrally dense pattern raises concern for parosteal osteosarcoma.

title: Early MO can look alarming before it matures
body: Before mature peripheral bone forms, MO can have substantial surrounding muscle edema and a painful mass. MRI may show a peripheral low-signal rim but is less decisive for mineralization than CT. Premature biopsy can be misleading; when imaging is characteristic, communicate the likely diagnosis and seek appropriate imaging correlation.
prompt: Why can MRI alone make early MO harder to classify?
answer: Edema can dominate and a low-signal rim may be nonspecific; radiographs or CT better demonstrate the diagnostic peripheral mineralization pattern.

title: Apophyseal avulsion can imitate aggressive tumor
body: An avulsion injury at a characteristic tendon attachment, such as the ischial tuberosity or AIIS, can show indistinct cortex, resorption, and productive bone. Healing may resemble an aggressive periosteal response. Location, maturity, and evolution on appropriately selected follow-up help avoid an unnecessary and potentially misleading biopsy.
prompt: A painful adolescent ischial lesion appears to have a Codman-like margin. What mimic should be checked?
answer: An apophyseal avulsion injury at the hamstring attachment; identify its characteristic location and healing behavior before calling a sarcoma.

title: Distal femoral cortical irregularity is a traction phenomenon
body: A tug lesion at the medial gastrocnemius origin can cause posterior-medial distal-femoral cortical indistinctness and productive change. DFCI is preferred to the misleading term cortical desmoid. This shares a general neighborhood with parosteal osteosarcoma, so recognize the attachment-centered pattern without ignoring an atypical enlarging mass.
prompt: What is the common benign explanation for attachment-centered posterior-medial femoral cortical irregularity in an adolescent?
answer: DFCI or a tug lesion at the medial gastrocnemius origin, rather than a true desmoid tumor.

title: Asymmetric ischiopubic closure is physiologic
body: One ischiopubic synchondrosis can enlarge and fuse later than the opposite side, producing an apparent expansile lucency during childhood. This van Neck-Odelberg pattern is related to asymmetric loading and maturation and often occurs opposite the dominant foot. Recognizing its precise location prevents a normal growth process from being treated as tumor.
prompt: What benign developmental process can create a unilateral expansile-looking ischiopubic lesion?
answer: Asymmetric maturation and delayed closure of the ischiopubic synchondrosis, known as the van Neck-Odelberg pattern.

title: Exuberant fracture callus can imitate osteoid tumor
body: A radiographically occult or inadequately immobilized fracture may generate marked sclerosis and immature periosteal callus that resembles osteosarcoma. Inspect for subtle cortical or physeal offset, consider stress injury, and review the injury history. Productive healing bone must be interpreted as part of a fracture pattern, not simply as matrix.
prompt: What subtle findings can rescue an apparent osteoid-producing tumor diagnosis in a recently injured adolescent?
answer: A fracture line, cortical or physeal offset, and a coherent callus distribution or interval healing pattern.

title: Healing first resorbs, then produces bone
body: Early resorption around a fracture can create a band-like lucency and make an ordinary fracture look pathologic. Later callus fills it in. The chapter illustrates a suspected sternal metastasis in a patient with cancer that was resolved by multiplanar evaluation and short-interval healing, showing why cancer history does not override geometry.
prompt: What configuration favors fracture-related resorption over an expansile tumor in the sternum?
answer: A band-like lucency centered on a fracture with an appropriate healing pattern; targeted interval imaging may show progressive bone fill.

title: Old trauma and subperiosteal hematoma leave odd shapes
body: Remote fracture remodeling can leave unusual osseous deformity. An old subperiosteal hematoma may become a mature ossified structure adherent to the bone surface. Seek mature architecture and a coherent traumatic explanation, while distinguishing it from a new mineralized soft-tissue mass.
prompt: What benign process can explain mature surface ossification along an old injured femoral shaft?
answer: An ossified and remodeled subperiosteal hematoma; mature architecture and clinical history support the interpretation.

title: A surgical tract may be the entire explanation
body: Biceps tenodesis can leave a proximal-humeral cortical or lucent defect without an obvious metallic anchor. FDL transfer or posterior-tibial tendon surgery can leave a navicular tract; the iliac crest may show graft-harvest defects. Correlate with surgery and nearby hardware before building a tumor differential.
prompt: Which prior procedures should you ask about for a humeral or navicular lucency?
answer: Biceps tenodesis for the humerus, and tendon repair or transfer such as FDL transfer for the navicular; check for nearby surgical clues.

title: Endplate-related sclerosis may remain degenerative when rounded
body: Degenerative discogenic sclerosis usually parallels vertebral endplates but can look rounded. Matched changes around the most degenerative disc level support a mechanical explanation. Assess the disc, opposing endplates, and regional pattern rather than labeling every rounded vertebral sclerotic focus a metastasis.
prompt: What distribution supports discogenic sclerosis over isolated blastic metastasis?
answer: Opposing endplate sclerosis centered on a conspicuously degenerative disc level, even if one component is somewhat rounded.

title: A large subchondral hole may be a geode
body: Degenerative subchondral cystic change can become very large and resemble tumor. Look for nonuniform joint-space loss, osteophytes, joint bodies, and mechanical buttressing. The arthritic joint provides the explanatory context; lesion size alone should not displace it. This is a major overlap with the end-of-bone tumor differential.
prompt: What accompanying findings favor geode over an epiphyseal tumor?
answer: An arthritic joint with osteophytes, asymmetric joint-space loss, joint bodies, or buttressing corresponding to subchondral cystic change.

title: Anterosuperior femoral-neck fibrocystic change has a typical address
body: Small rounded lucencies with sclerotic margins at the anterosuperior femoral neck represent a characteristic benign fibrocystic process, formerly termed herniation or Pitt pits. They are more prevalent with femoroacetabular impingement but also occur in asymptomatic people; their presence alone does not diagnose symptomatic FAI.
prompt: Does a femoral-neck herniation pit prove that hip symptoms are caused by FAI?
answer: No. Such pits also occur in asymptomatic patients and must be interpreted with the complete clinical and morphologic picture.

title: Dorsal patellar defect is location-driven
body: A lucent defect in the upper outer patella near the articular surface is a recognizable developmental variant. MRI can show low T1 and high T2 signal with preserved, sometimes puckered, overlying cartilage. Its characteristic site distinguishes it from a generic patellar epiphyseal-equivalent tumor.
prompt: Where must you look for a dorsal defect of the patella?
answer: The upper outer or superolateral patella near its articular surface; location is the key clue.

title: Greater-tuberosity pseudocyst is not a true mass
body: Normal regional cancellous-versus-cortical proportions can make the greater tuberosity look lucent, accentuated by hyperemia or disuse. Cross-sectional imaging does not show a corresponding true lesion. A real chondroblastoma can occur nearby, so require a coherent lesion and not location alone before dismissing an abnormality.
prompt: How can you distinguish a greater-tuberosity pseudocyst from a true tumor in the same region?
answer: Look for a reproducible bounded lesion, a true sclerotic rim or mass, and cross-sectional confirmation; a pseudocyst lacks a corresponding structural lesion.

title: The calcaneal trabecular gap can mimic a cyst
body: Normal calcaneal trabecular arches create an anteroinferior lucent region beneath the critical angle of Gissane. Unlike a true simple cyst or lipoma in the same neighborhood, the pseudolesion is more indistinct and does not form a discrete structural mass. Recognize the normal architecture before labeling pathology.
prompt: What favors a calcaneal pseudocyst rather than a simple bone cyst?
answer: Indistinct normal trabecular boundaries rather than a true sharply bounded lesion in the characteristic calcaneal location.

title: Bone island has cortical-bone architecture in marrow
body: A bone island is a focus of compact bone in the medullary cavity. It may be oblong along the stress axis and have fine spiculated margins blending into trabeculae. Near-joint location and cortical-like density support the diagnosis; on MRI it is dark across routine sequences.
prompt: Which morphological clues favor bone island over a blastic metastasis?
answer: A very dense compact-bone focus with brush-like spiculated margins, an oblong stress-axis orientation, and an otherwise typical juxta-articular context.

title: Density, slow growth, and uptake require context
body: A fixed CT attenuation threshold does not reliably settle every bone-island-versus-metastasis problem. Large bone islands can show low-level scintigraphic uptake and can grow slowly. Evaluate the complete morphology, comparisons, and clinical setting instead of treating one HU number, any growth, or any uptake as decisive.
prompt: Does slow enlargement or mild MDP uptake rule out a bone island?
answer: No. Both can occur; compare morphology and the full clinical context, and do not rely on a single HU cutoff.

title: Osteopoikilosis is patterned multiplicity of bone islands
body: Numerous small dense bone islands clustered around joints suggest osteopoikilosis, often an incidental asymptomatic finding. Their distribution and long-axis orientation are helpful when the number seems alarming. The pattern differs from an unstructured assumption of widespread blastic metastases.
prompt: What distribution makes numerous small sclerotic lesions reassuring for osteopoikilosis?
answer: A characteristic juxta-articular clustering of bone islands, often with their long axes aligned with local stress directions.

title: Bone infarct has a serpiginous peripheral boundary
body: Metadiaphyseal osteonecrosis is termed a bone infarct. Its serpentine peripheral sclerosis differs from the internal rings, arcs, or lobular flocculent mineralization of enchondroma. Small examples can remain equivocal on radiographs, in which case a differential is more honest than an overconfident label.
prompt: How does mineralization distribution distinguish infarct from enchondroma?
answer: Infarct tends to have a serpiginous peripheral sclerotic rim; enchondroma has internal chondroid mineralization rather than a strictly peripheral linear border.

title: Paget disease alters the whole bone architecture
body: Paget disease usually involves a sizable segment of bone with expansion, cortical thickening, and coarse trabeculae in an older patient. Skull, spine, pelvis, and proximal appendicular sites are common. Patchy rounded medullary sclerosis can obscure the classic pattern; assess the bone's size and cortex rather than only the sclerotic foci.
prompt: What three architectural findings help separate Paget disease from a blastic metastasis?
answer: Bone expansion, cortical thickening, and trabecular coarsening in a characteristic regional distribution.

title: Avid Paget disease can imitate metastatic activity
body: Paget disease can show increased FDG and MDP uptake. In a patient with cancer, tracer avidity should therefore be read alongside morphology rather than overriding expansion, thick cortex, and the characteristic distribution. The symptomatic side may even be different from the incidental Pagetic bone.
prompt: Does FDG avidity turn a morphologically classic Pagetic lesion into a metastasis?
answer: No. Paget disease can be metabolically active on FDG PET and bone scintigraphy; morphology and distribution remain essential.

title: Infection can span the entire behavior spectrum
body: Acute osteomyelitis may be permeative and aggressive, a Brodie abscess may be a sharply bordered lucency, and chronic infection may be densely sclerotic. Periosteal reaction and marrow or soft-tissue inflammation can add further overlap with tumors. Search for joint involvement, tunnels, and abscess architecture rather than relying on one pattern.
prompt: Why is infection a necessary alternative for both an aggressive and an apparently indolent bone lesion?
answer: Its appearance changes with phase and form, from acute permeative destruction to a rimmed abscess or chronic sclerosis.

title: Brodie abscess is a physeal-adjacent mimic in the young
body: Brodie abscess commonly presents near a physis in a skeletally immature patient as a geographic lucency with a sclerotic rim. An elongated shape or tract-like projection can help. Thick reactive sclerosis, periosteal bone, and nocturnal pain can overlap OO, so seek the cavity and infection-specific architecture.
prompt: What favors Brodie abscess over an uncomplicated OO pattern?
answer: An elongated or tract-like medullary cavity near a physis, abscess-related MRI features, and cortical drainage tracts rather than only a small round nidus.

title: The penumbra sign supports abscess
body: A thin rim of relatively increased T1 signal surrounding an abscess cavity is the penumbra sign. In the appropriate morphology it strongly supports intraosseous abscess. Identify it on T1-weighted imaging and distinguish it from the nonspecific surrounding T2 edema that many tumors and irritators can produce.
prompt: What sequence and finding define the penumbra sign?
answer: A relatively T1-bright rim at the periphery of the low-signal abscess cavity, rather than simply diffuse T2-bright edema.

title: Tunnels and a cloaca are clues to pus
body: A cortical drainage tract into soft tissues is a cloaca. Irregular tunnels through cortex or bulky periosteal new bone support chronic infection, which can otherwise resemble a surface tumor. Thick circumferential consolidated periosteal bone may produce a bone-in-bone appearance; chronic sclerosis can be very substantial.
prompt: What is a cloaca, and why is it useful in a tumor differential?
answer: A tract draining an intraosseous infectious focus through cortex toward soft tissue; it supports infection rather than a generic surface or intramedullary tumor.

title: CRMO is sterile inflammatory osteitis
body: In children and adolescents, CRMO can be unifocal or multifocal and cause periosteal new bone, sclerosis, and variable lysis, closely resembling infection or Ewing sarcoma. The clavicle is a characteristic site. Tissue sampling is often used to exclude infection when the presentation is not sufficiently characteristic.
prompt: What important noninfectious mimic can produce chronic-osteomyelitis-like changes in a child's clavicle?
answer: CRMO, a sterile inflammatory osteitis that can be solitary or multifocal.

title: Disuse osteoporosis can look permeative
body: Regional osteoporosis with cortical tunneling may imitate a destructive tumor, especially when one proximal humerus differs markedly from the other. In a hemiparetic patient, review stroke history and side of weakness; shoulder pain may arise from loss of muscle tone and capsular strain rather than a focal tumor.
prompt: What history can explain apparent unilateral permeative proximal-humeral change without a mass?
answer: Hemiparesis and disuse after a contralateral cerebral infarct, with regional osteoporosis and cortical tunneling.

title: Recognize when the best answer is a mimic
body: Before proposing biopsy, check for a characteristic developmental, traumatic, degenerative, vascular, or postoperative explanation. Some mimics are diagnosable on imaging, and healing tissue or early MO can even mislead histology. When imaging and pathology disagree, communicate the lesion's location and pattern rather than accepting either in isolation.
prompt: What useful role does the radiologist have beyond listing tumor names?
answer: Identifying a specific benign mimic, avoiding unnecessary workup when the pattern is characteristic, and resolving imaging-pathology discordance with the treating team.

title: An isolated lesser-trochanter fracture is a red flag in adults
body: The chapter illustrates an isolated lesser-trochanter fracture over a destructive RCC metastasis. In an adult, this should prompt careful evaluation for an underlying lesion rather than reflexively assuming a sports-related apophyseal avulsion. Search the parent proximal femur and correlate the age and cancer history.
prompt: What should you look for beneath an isolated lesser-trochanter fracture in an older adult?
answer: An underlying destructive lesion or metastasis causing a pathologic fracture.

title: An older patient's GCT-like lesion can be metastasis
body: A geographic subarticular lytic mass can satisfy several GCT imaging clues and still be metastatic disease. The chapter's example is an elderly patient with RCC and a pathologic fracture. The answer should integrate morphology with prior malignancy and age rather than allowing a classic-looking location to erase the history.
prompt: A 77-year-old with RCC has a GCT-like epiphyseal lesion. What should lead the differential?
answer: Metastatic RCC deserves priority because the age and history substantially change the likelihood, despite overlapping GCT morphology.

title: Use discriminators to shorten, not inflate, the list
body: A mnemonic is useful for recalling names but does not substitute for a case-specific impression. Narrow by maturity, actual epicenter, matrix, border, and host response, then explain the leading diagnosis and critical alternative. The chapter explicitly treats its discriminators as high-confidence practical tools with exceptions.
prompt: How should you answer a request for a differential after completing the description?
answer: Give a short prioritized list supported by the strongest age, location, and behavior clues, including a consequential mimic or malignant alternative where appropriate.

title: Use interval change to answer a specific unresolved question
body: Comparison can show NOF involution, healing callus, or resolution of fracture-related resorption. Slow bone-island enlargement is also possible, so any growth is not a universal malignancy rule. If interval imaging is used, explain what expected maturation or structural change would support the proposed diagnosis rather than merely saying follow-up.
prompt: What should a useful follow-up recommendation clarify in an indeterminate but possibly healing lesion?
answer: The specific suspected process and expected change, such as consolidation or filling of a fracture-related lucency; timing and modality depend on the actual case.

title: Score five imaging findings and one clinical factor
body: Review margination, periosteal reaction, endosteal erosion, pathological fracture, extra-osseous soft tissue mass, and a history of primary cancer. Assign the relevant point value in each domain and add all six. Do not substitute matrix, lesion density, or a favored diagnosis for these scoring domains.
prompt: What are the six scoring elements?
answer: Margin; periosteal reaction; endosteal erosion; pathological fracture; extra-osseous mass; primary-cancer history.

title: Point total and Bone-RADS category are different numbers
body: A total of 1-2 points maps to Bone-RADS 1, very low risk; 3-4 points to category 2, low risk; 5-6 points to category 3, intermediate risk; and 7 or more points to category 4, high risk. Category 0 means incomplete characterization, not a calculated total of zero. State both the sum and its category to avoid ambiguity.
prompt: A lesion totals 5 points. What is its Bone-RADS score?
answer: Bone-RADS 3, intermediate risk. Five is the summed point total, not the category.

title: Margin provides the baseline 1, 3, 5, or 7 points
body: In the modified Lodwick-Madewell system used here, IA is geographic and sharply defined with marginal sclerosis (1 point); IB is geographic and sharply defined without a complete sclerotic margin (3); II is geographic but ill defined (5); and IIIA-C represents changing, nongeographic, or invisible margins (7). Evaluate the entire lesion rather than its most reassuring segment.
prompt: Which margin types alone reach the high-risk category?
answer: Modified grades IIIA, IIIB, and IIIC each contribute 7 points and therefore reach Bone-RADS 4.

title: Specify whether Lodwick terminology is original or modified
body: Original Lodwick IC means geographic but ill-defined destruction; this is modified grade II. Original grade II describes moth-eaten destruction and original III describes permeative destruction; the modified system groups both as IIIB. The same numeral can therefore describe a different pattern. Use words plus the named grading system during a case presentation.
prompt: Is modified grade II the same as original Lodwick grade II?
answer: No. Modified II is geographic and ill defined, corresponding to original IC. Original moth-eaten II is modified IIIB.

title: Do not attach precise cancer percentages to the full score
body: The paper cites a retrospective study of 183 osteolytic lesions supporting the modified margin classification: grade I had less than 10% malignancy, grade II approximately 50%, and grade III more than 80%. These are results for margin groups in that study. They are not validated probability estimates for the complete six-domain Bone-RADS categories.
prompt: What do the less-than-10%, approximately-50%, and greater-than-80% figures describe?
answer: Modified Lodwick-Madewell margin grades I, II, and III in the cited retrospective study, not calibrated probabilities for the composite Bone-RADS score.

title: A changing margin can reveal the most active component
body: Modified IIIA describes changing or combined margins, such as a lesion with one sharply defined segment and another poorly defined segment. This may reflect malignant transformation of a pre-existing benign lesion. Assign the grade that reflects the most concerning destruction pattern; a reassuring portion does not neutralize the aggressive portion.
prompt: Why inspect every margin of a long-standing lesion?
answer: A new aggressive component can coexist with an old indolent component; the highest-concern margin governs the assessment.

title: Radiographically invisible margins do not exclude aggressive tumor
body: Modified IIIC covers lesions detected by other imaging that remain occult or have invisible margins on radiographs. Infiltrative tumor can advance through marrow and cancellous bone before host osteoclastic destruction becomes radiographically visible. Distinguish this established occult infiltrative lesion from a poorly visualized finding that is simply not yet characterized and needs Bone-RADS 0 workup.
prompt: How can an aggressive marrow lesion have little visible osteolysis?
answer: Tumor infiltration can outpace the host bone-resorption response; MRI or other modalities may reveal disease not delineated by radiographs.

title: Periosteal reaction adds 0, 2, or 4 points
body: No periosteal reaction contributes 0; nonaggressive reaction contributes 2; aggressive reaction contributes 4. Describe the pattern before assigning the points. Periosteal reaction reflects growth rate and host response, so it supports biologic activity rather than proving a specific histology.
prompt: How many points does aggressive periosteal reaction add?
answer: Four, compared with two for nonaggressive reaction and zero for none.

title: Measure endosteal scalloping relative to cortical thickness
body: Mild erosion is less than one-third of cortical thickness and adds 0 points; moderate erosion is between one-third and two-thirds and adds 1; deep/severe erosion exceeds two-thirds or includes cortical disruption and adds 2. More extensive erosion suggests greater biologic activity. The article does not define how to assign an exact boundary measurement, so avoid implying false precision.
prompt: A medullary lesion erodes more than two-thirds of the cortex. How is that scored?
answer: Deep or severe endosteal erosion, adding 2 points.

title: Assess fracture risk separately from malignancy risk
body: Every bone lesion should be evaluated for impending or existing pathological fracture. Orthogonal radiographs assess lesion density, location, extent of cortical involvement, and relation to articular surfaces; symptoms matter as well. Mirels uses size/cortical involvement, location, density, and pain. Bone-RADS and fracture-risk assessment answer different management questions.
prompt: Does a low malignancy category eliminate the need to evaluate mechanical risk?
answer: No. A benign lesion can weaken bone enough to require orthopedic management. Mirels incorporates pain, site, lesion density, and cortical involvement.

title: An extra-osseous mass adds 4 points
body: A soft tissue mass contributes 4 points, not 2. Look for cortical breakthrough, focal cortical or periosteal discontinuity, soft tissue fullness, altered fat planes, asymmetry, and increased soft tissue density. MRI is substantially better than radiography at showing soft tissue extension. In a cartilaginous lesion, new extra-osseous extension may be an early sign of malignant transformation.
prompt: How many points does an extra-osseous soft tissue mass add, and what best delineates it?
answer: Four points; MRI generally delineates its extent better than radiography.

title: Primary-cancer history changes the same radiographic calculation
body: Known primary cancer contributes 2 points; absence of that history contributes 0. A well-defined geographic lesion without a complete sclerotic rim starts at 3 margin points; adding a cancer history produces 5 points and category 3 even before other concerning findings. History is an explicit scoring element, while the probability of metastasis still needs clinical judgment.
prompt: What happens to a 3-point IB lesion when the patient has a known primary cancer?
answer: The added 2 points yield a total of 5 and Bone-RADS 3, intermediate risk.

title: Ask whether sclerosis is host response, matrix, or a recognizable pattern
body: Sclerosis may reflect reactive bone or intrinsic tumor matrix. Consider healing fracture, treatment response, osteoid osteoma/osteoblastoma, osteosarcoma, osteoblastic metastases, lymphoma, and chronic osteomyelitis. Linear sclerosis can suggest healing fracture; a serpentine rim favors osteonecrosis. Mixed ill-defined lysis and patchy sclerosis can occur in lymphoma. Common osteoblastic metastases include prostate, breast, urothelial, and neuroendocrine tumors.
prompt: Why is a sclerotic focus not automatically an osteoid-producing tumor?
answer: The density may be a reactive host response, a healing process, metastasis, or another pathology rather than intrinsic osteoid matrix.

title: Recognize osteoid versus chondroid mineralization
body: Cloudlike or amorphous mineralization suggests osteoid production and supports a bone-forming lineage such as osteoid osteoma, osteoblastoma, or osteosarcoma. Rings-and-arcs, flocculent, or flecklike calcification in a lobulated medullary lesion suggests cartilage. Matrix suggests lineage; it does not by itself determine benignity or grade.
prompt: What does rings-and-arcs mineralization establish, and what does it not establish?
answer: It supports cartilaginous matrix; it does not alone distinguish enchondroma from chondrosarcoma.

title: Use distinctive site predilections as discriminators
body: The paper highlights anterior proximal-to-mid tibial cortex for adamantinoma and the posterior distal femoral surface for parosteal osteosarcoma. Multiple well-circumscribed lytic lesions in the small tubular bones of the hand favor enchondromas. Location refines a differential after the lesion has been described and risk assessed.
prompt: What are two classic site clues for adamantinoma and parosteal osteosarcoma?
answer: Adamantinoma: anterior cortex of proximal-to-mid tibia. Parosteal osteosarcoma: posterior surface of distal femur.

title: Bone-RADS 0: characterize before assigning risk
body: Use category 0 when a lesion is incompletely seen or evaluated. Overlapping anatomy commonly limits assessment in the scapula, spine, and pelvis. Obtain additional views or cross-sectional imaging before giving a malignancy-risk category. A limited study is not reassuring merely because its most aggressive features cannot be demonstrated.
prompt: What is the correct category when overlying anatomy prevents margin and cortex assessment?
answer: Bone-RADS 0, with additional imaging to characterize the lesion before risk assignment.

title: Bone-RADS 1: classic benign lesions still need symptom context
body: At 1-2 points, the lesion is very likely benign. A classic asymptomatic lesion may need no further workup, or annual surveillance may be considered to confirm expected stability. New pain, fracture, or other clinical change can justify further imaging or orthopedic oncology review. Treatment may be needed for symptoms even when malignancy risk is very low.
prompt: How can management differ between an asymptomatic and symptomatic category 1 lesion?
answer: The asymptomatic classic lesion may be observed or discharged; symptoms or change can require imaging and referral for treatment.

title: Bone-RADS 2: surveillance is often 3-6 months
body: At 3-4 points, the lesion is probably benign. For an asymptomatic case, consider short-interval radiographic surveillance in 3-6 months. Advanced imaging can clarify composition and activity; selected cases may need biopsy for diagnostic confidence. Symptomatic or locally aggressive benign tumors, including giant cell tumor, may need orthopedic oncology treatment despite a low malignancy category.
prompt: What is the suggested initial surveillance interval for an asymptomatic category 2 lesion?
answer: Three to six months, with further evaluation if the lesion changes or clinical circumstances warrant it.

title: Bone-RADS 3: characterize and coordinate probable biopsy
body: At 5-6 points, the lesion is potentially malignant and may be radiographically indeterminate. The paper recommends orthopedic oncology referral, advanced imaging for characterization and planning, and often image-guided or surgical biopsy. Infection remains a competing diagnosis in the correct setting. A known cancer history can push an otherwise geographic lesion into this category.
prompt: What is the next-step framework for a category 3 lesion?
answer: Orthopedic oncology review, appropriate advanced imaging, and probable biopsy coordinated with the treating team.

title: Bone-RADS 4: treat as malignant until proven otherwise
body: At 7 or more points, the lesion is highly suspicious. Refer to orthopedic oncology for assessment, confirmatory biopsy, treatment planning, and staging imaging, including evaluation for additional disease as appropriate. Examples include a nongeographic moth-eaten/permeative lesion or combinations of geographic destruction with other aggressive features. The category conveys concern, not a tissue diagnosis.
prompt: What follows a category 4 assessment?
answer: Orthopedic oncology referral, coordinated biopsy, staging, and treatment planning.

title: Plan the biopsy with the team providing definitive treatment
body: For a potentially malignant lesion, the article recommends that biopsy be performed in consultation with the orthopedic oncologist who would provide definitive treatment. Advanced imaging helps characterize the lesion and plan treatment. A case answer should therefore pair the need for tissue with specialist coordination, rather than offering an isolated biopsy recommendation without a plan.
prompt: Why mention orthopedic oncology when recommending biopsy?
answer: The diagnostic procedure should be coordinated with the team that will provide definitive oncologic treatment.

title: Fig. 6: a hidden scapular lesion becomes plasmacytoma on CT
body: The right shoulder radiograph partly obscures an osteolytic scapular lesion behind the humeral head; margins and cortical breakthrough cannot be evaluated confidently. This is Bone-RADS 0. CT reveals destructive disease with an extra-osseous mass, and biopsy confirms plasmacytoma. The teaching point is inadequate initial characterization, not a low-risk radiographic appearance.
prompt: In Fig. 6, why is the radiograph category 0 despite the serious eventual diagnosis?
answer: Overlying anatomy prevents complete assessment. CT then exposes destructive tumor and extra-osseous extension.

title: Fig. 7: a classic nonossifying fibroma totals 1 point
body: A 15-year-old girl has an eccentric distal tibial lesion with circumferential marginal sclerosis. It is modified grade IA (1 point), with 0 in the remaining domains: total 1, Bone-RADS 1. Recognize the classic appearance of a nonossifying fibroma and then state symptom-appropriate management.
prompt: What contributes the single point in the nonossifying fibroma example?
answer: The IA margin; every other scoring feature contributes zero.

title: Fig. 8: 3 margin points plus 1 erosion point gives category 2
body: A 59-year-old woman has a geographic proximal tibial lucency with incomplete marginal sclerosis (modified IB) and moderate medial scalloping. Margins contribute 3 and erosion 1: total 4, category 2. Age prompted laboratory assessment and MRI; MRI demonstrated a simple-appearing unicameral cyst with mild cortical thinning and minimal periostitis. Do not dismiss an unusual-age lesion on appearance alone.
prompt: Why is Fig. 8 a 4-point lesion rather than a 1-point IA lesion?
answer: Its marginal sclerosis is incomplete, making it IB (3), and moderate scalloping adds 1.

title: Corrected Fig. 9: an aggressive feature can outweigh a sclerotic rim
body: The elderly patient with remote femoral plate fixation has a geographic lucency with hazy marginal sclerosis and lamellated periosteal reaction. Correct scoring is IA margin 1 plus aggressive periosteal reaction 4, with all other features 0: total 5, category 3. Biopsy and positive cultures establish Brodie abscess. The 2024 correction on PDF page 17 supersedes the original page-13 graphic.
prompt: What is the corrected score, and what diagnosis explains the aggressive appearance?
answer: 1 + 4 = 5 points, Bone-RADS 3; Brodie abscess. Infection can produce aggressive periosteal reaction despite a sclerotic margin.

title: Fig. 10: ill-defined geographic destruction plus fracture reaches category 4
body: A 66-year-old man without known malignancy has elbow pain, an ill-defined geographic distal humeral lesion, and pathological cortical fractures. Modified II margins add 5 and fracture adds 2: total 7, Bone-RADS 4. Biopsy shows poorly differentiated carcinoma; subsequent workup identifies additional osseous and visceral disease. An absent cancer history does not exclude metastatic disease.
prompt: How does the distal humeral lesion reach high risk without a known primary cancer?
answer: Five points for ill-defined geographic margins plus two for pathological fracture reaches seven, category 4.

title: Apply the consensus framework without inventing validation
body: The committee selected individual point weights by expert consensus, and explicitly states that future validation would be beneficial. Management combines published evidence, best practice, and expert opinion. The modified margin classification has cited retrospective data, but that does not validate the entire composite score. Use clinical context and disclose incomplete characterization rather than treating the score as an infallible diagnostic calculator.
prompt: What is the main evidence limitation of the six-domain point system?
answer: Its point weights were established by expert consensus and need validation; the composite categories do not supply validated absolute malignancy probabilities.

title: Use the corrected Fig. 9 graphic when learning the scoring table
body: The original Fig. 9 graphic on PDF page 13 incorrectly displays 1 endosteal-erosion point even though its caption says all non-margin/non-periosteal domains are zero; it also mislabels a positive soft tissue mass as 2 points. The corrected graphic on page 17 shows erosion 0 and a mass worth 4, matching Table 1. The correct example remains total 5 and category 3. Preserve the historical image only with its correction clearly visible.
prompt: Which source should control if the original Fig. 9 diagram conflicts with Table 1?
answer: Table 1 and corrected Fig. 9: soft tissue mass is 4 points, this example has erosion 0, and 1 margin + 4 periosteal = 5.

title: Choose the next modality for the unanswered question
body: The exhibit starts with radiographs. CT clarifies small mineralized foci, cortex, periosteal new bone, and fractures; MRI shows marrow extent, soft tissue involvement, enhancement, and local staging. Bone scintigraphy can survey skeletal activity, but the appropriate wider workup depends on the suspected disease. Match a proposed next study to the finding you need to resolve.
prompt: When would CT add more than another radiograph, and when would MRI add more?
answer: CT for subtle matrix and cortical detail; MRI for marrow extent, soft tissues, and local staging.

title: Age narrows a differential, but the age table contains an error
body: The younger group includes cysts, nonossifying fibroma, osteofibrous dysplasia, chondroblastoma, osteoblastoma, and LCH, with osteosarcoma and Ewing sarcoma among important malignancies. In older adults prioritize metastasis, myeloma, and chondrosarcoma when a lesion is suspicious. Slide 6 incorrectly places chondroblastoma in its older malignant list; chondroblastoma should remain in the benign tumor differential. The same slide prose correctly says chondrosarcoma.
prompt: Which similarly named tumors must you keep distinct when reading slide 6?
answer: Chondroblastoma is generally a benign cartilage tumor; chondrosarcoma is malignant. The older malignant column has a labeling error.

title: Cotton-wool skull and expanded coarse-trabecular bone suggest Paget disease
body: Compare the 55-year-old woman with thickened calvarium and patchy cotton-wool sclerosis on slide 7 with the mixed-density expanded distal femur on slide 17. Cortical thickening, coarse trabeculae, and expansion organize the diagnosis beyond simply calling the lesion mixed or sclerotic. Age and the distribution of involvement help distinguish this remodeling disorder from focal tumor.
prompt: What combination makes the mixed femoral appearance more suggestive of Paget disease?
answer: Bone expansion, cortical thickening, and coarse trabeculae, interpreted with the age and distribution.

title: A classic nonossifying fibroma can still fracture
body: The 8-year-old girl on slide 7 has an eccentric proximal tibial lucency with a sharply sclerotic border, open physes, and an associated pathological fracture. The appearance supports nonossifying fibroma while the fracture creates a separate management problem. The later case on slide 57 illustrates a nonfractured distal femoral NOF with moderate scalloping.
prompt: What should you say after recognizing the classic NOF in the child with leg pain?
answer: Describe the fracture and assess mechanical risk. A benign diagnosis does not make the fracture incidental.

title: A beveled skull lucency in a child is a useful LCH case
body: The skull radiograph in a 2-year-old child shows a lytic lesion with beveled edges, illustrating eosinophilic granuloma/Langerhans cell histiocytosis. The exhibit identifies the skeleton as a common site of LCH and the skull as a frequent osseous location. The diagnostic argument should use age, skull location, and the characteristic edge rather than the lucency alone.
prompt: Which three clues support LCH in the skull case?
answer: Very young age, calvarial location, and beveled edges of a lytic defect.

title: An enchondroma in a phalanx can scallop and lack obvious calcification
body: The proximal phalangeal enchondroma on slide 9 produces endosteal scalloping. The caption cautions that hand enchondromas may have little or no calcified matrix, although the illustrated case has visible mineralization. A phalangeal lucency therefore need not show abundant rings and arcs to belong to the cartilage family.
prompt: Does absent chondroid calcification exclude an enchondroma in the hand?
answer: No. Hand enchondromas may lack conspicuous calcified matrix; site and morphology remain useful.

title: Use the epicenter, not the total footprint, to describe location
body: Slide 11 pairs a centrally located distal femoral enchondroma and rib LCH lesion with an eccentric distal femoral NOF. Slide 12 contrasts intracortical osteoid osteoma in the humerus with a surface osteosarcoma arising from the proximal tibia. Name the epicenter on orthogonal views before using the site to narrow the differential.

answer: An intracortical epicenter versus an external, juxtacortical/surface epicenter.

title: Combine skeletal maturity with epiphyseal location
body: The longitudinal-location diagram places chondroblastoma in the younger epiphyseal differential and giant cell tumor in the older group. The accompanying distal tibial GCT case reaches the epiphysis, while the femoral chondrosarcoma example is metaphyseal with chondroid matrix and cortical breakthrough. Use age, physis status, and lesion behavior together rather than treating epiphyseal location as a diagnosis.

answer: Patient age and skeletal maturity, along with margin, matrix, and cortical behavior.

title: Two sclerotic lesions can represent very different processes
body: Slide 15 contrasts an ivory L3 vertebral body caused by breast-cancer metastasis with an eccentric healed NOF in the distal femoral metaphysis. The distribution and underlying pattern matter: diffuse vertebral sclerosis and a healed eccentric metaphyseal lesion should not enter the same unfiltered differential merely because both are dense.
prompt: Why should the healed NOF and ivory vertebra be approached differently?
answer: Their bone, distribution, and morphology differ; sclerosis is an appearance shared by unrelated processes.

title: A broad lucent-lesion mnemonic is a starting list
body: Slide 16 uses FEGNOMASHIC for geographic lucencies: fibrous dysplasia; enchondroma/LCH; GCT/geode; NOF; osteoblastoma; metastasis/myeloma; ABC; simple cyst; brown tumor/hemangioma; infection/infarction; chondroblastoma/chondromyxoid fibroma. Filter this list using age, site, matrix, and host response. Its inclusion of malignancy and infection is a reminder that geographic appearance alone does not settle etiology.
prompt: Which serious categories remain in a geographic lucent-lesion differential?
answer: Metastasis, myeloma, and infection, among others. Narrow margins do not remove the clinical context.

body: The radius metastasis caption calls the lucency well defined while assigning original Lodwick IC. In the exhibit comparison table, original IC means geographic but ill defined, corresponding to modified II. Treat the caption as inconsistent and inspect the image rather than learning that IC is a well-defined subtype. This is also a reminder to name the original versus modified system.

answer: Geographic but ill defined, with a wide transition. It maps to modified Lodwick-Madewell II.

title: No visible matrix leaves both metastasis and round-cell tumor in play
body: Slide 18 pairs a sharply bounded lytic skull metastasis from lung cancer with a lytic pubic lesion in a 12-year-old with Ewing sarcoma; neither has recognizable mineralized matrix. Elsewhere the same slide illustrates cloudlike osteoid in osteosarcoma. Treat absent mineralization as descriptive information rather than evidence against malignancy.
prompt: What do the skull metastasis and pubic Ewing lesion teach about absent matrix?
answer: A malignant lesion may have no radiographically mineralized matrix.

title: Compare rings and arcs with ground-glass density
body: Slide 19 compares an enchondroma with an atypical cartilaginous tumor that has endosteal scalloping, both showing chondroid mineralization. It also shows fibrous dysplasia in the proximal femur and parietal bone with hazy ground-glass density and remodeling. Ground glass and cartilage calcification guide lineage, while cortical behavior and the clinical setting determine concern.

answer: Both enchondroma and ACT can mineralize as rings and arcs; scalloping, site, symptoms, and other features supply the distinction.

title: A sclerotic rim can occur in fibrous dysplasia or a toe osteoblastoma
body: The IA examples on slide 21 include proximal femoral fibrous dysplasia and an osteoblastoma in the proximal phalanx of the great toe, both with a lucent center and sclerotic border. Their shared slow-growth margin does not make them the same lesion. The differential also includes Brodie abscess and several other benign entities.
