answer: The lesion is geographic with a sclerotic border, suggesting time for a host response. It does not specify one diagnosis.

title: Giant cell tumor can have sharp or aggressive margins
body: The distal femoral GCT on slide 22 has a sharp nonsclerotic IB margin. The distal tibial GCT on slide 23 is ill defined, alongside a telangiectatic osteosarcoma example with similarly aggressive geographic destruction. A known benign tumor family can show locally aggressive behavior, so base the initial management concern on the presented lesion.
prompt: Does an ill-defined geographic margin rule out giant cell tumor?
answer: No. GCT can be locally aggressive. A similar margin may also occur in malignant lesions such as telangiectatic osteosarcoma.

title: Use the pattern before forcing an exact histology
body: The moth-eaten example on slide 24 is myeloma in the skull. Slide 25 shows permeative destruction in a radial Ewing lesion and tibial lymphoma. These nongeographic patterns overlap sarcoma, plasma-cell disease, metastasis, infection, and LCH. Recognize the wide transition and destructive behavior before narrowing the differential using age and distribution.
prompt: Which two marrow-based malignant families are illustrated by permeative extremity lesions?
answer: Ewing sarcoma and lymphoma. The destruction pattern is aggressive but not specific.

title: Multiple lucencies expand the differential beyond common metastases
body: The four-view myeloma example on slide 26 demonstrates skull, humeral, spinal, and femoral disease in an older man. The broader polyostotic list includes metastases and lymphoma but also brown tumors, fibrous dysplasia, enchondromatosis, and vascular lesions. Survey distribution and correlate with laboratory/clinical information rather than assigning every multifocal lucency to metastatic carcinoma.
prompt: Name nonmetastatic explanations for multiple lytic lesions.
answer: Myeloma or lymphoma, brown tumors, fibrous dysplasia, enchondromatosis, and selected vascular disorders.

title: Osteopoikilosis and osteoblastic metastases can both be multifocal
body: Slide 27 juxtaposes numerous incidental bone islands in osteopoikilosis with multiple sclerotic pelvic metastases from a neuroendocrine tumor. The follow-up question is to assess the complete pattern and history rather than treating multiplicity plus sclerosis as automatically malignant. Neuroendocrine tumor joins the familiar prostate and breast primaries in the osteoblastic differential.
prompt: What benign mimic is shown next to the multifocal sclerotic metastases?
answer: Osteopoikilosis, consisting of multiple bone islands.

title: The lamellated pair directly compares Ewing with osteomyelitis
body: Slide 29 shows multilamellated reaction and a surrounding mass in femoral Ewing sarcoma, then radiograph/CT correlation of lamellated reaction in radial osteomyelitis. This paired example is useful when asked whether an aggressive periosteal response establishes cancer. It demonstrates the same growth-rate clue across malignant and infectious disease.
prompt: Which imaging pattern is shared by the Ewing and osteomyelitis examples?
answer: Lamellated or onion-skin periosteal reaction.
overlap: Visual application of a repeated principle: Lamellated reaction is aggressive but nonspecific.

title: Hair-on-end periosteal reaction can occur with metastasis
body: The illustrated parallel-spiculated examples on slide 30 are tibial metastases in a patient with prostate cancer, imaged at different times. Although this reaction commonly evokes Ewing sarcoma or osteosarcoma, the displayed cases show that it is not specific to a primary sarcoma. Say parallel spiculation, then interpret the age and history.
prompt: What unexpected cause of hair-on-end reaction is illustrated in the tibia?
answer: Prostate-cancer metastases.

title: CT can clarify a divergent periosteal response
body: Slide 31 pairs radiography and CT of iliac osteosarcoma with divergent spicules. The cross-sectional correlation helps separate the spiculated surface response from the lesion and overlying anatomy. Slide 32 then shows Codman triangles with femoral osteosarcomas; both are aggressive response patterns that still require etiologic interpretation.
prompt: How would you describe the periosteal pattern in the iliac case?
answer: Divergent spiculated or sunburst periosteal reaction, shown in osteosarcoma.

title: A cyst and a cartilage malignancy both erode the inner cortex
body: Slide 33 contrasts a central expansile humeral simple bone cyst in a 9-year-old with a chondroid proximal humeral lesion identified as chondrosarcoma. Both show endosteal scalloping. Characterize depth and extent, and integrate matrix and age. The presence of scalloping alone cannot identify cartilage malignancy.
prompt: Why does endosteal scalloping require more than a yes-or-no description?
answer: Its severity and context differ across benign cysts, benign cartilage lesions, and malignancies.
overlap: Visual application of a repeated principle: Scalloping is a pattern, not a diagnosis.

title: Inspect the growth plate and nearby bones in expansile cases
body: In slide 34, a proximal humeral simple bone cyst expands the metaphysis but does not cross the growth plate. The elbow example has several expansile lesions from polyostotic fibrous dysplasia, including a subtle proximal radial lesion. Use the physis and visible adjacent bones as deliberate search targets before concluding that a process is isolated.
prompt: What two search steps are emphasized by the remodeling examples?
answer: Determine whether the lesion crosses the physis, and inspect nearby bones for additional disease.

title: A destructive finger lesion can be an acrometastasis
body: Slide 35 shows cortical destruction in a proximal phalanx caused by lung-cancer metastasis. A second case illustrates proximal humeral angiosarcoma with complete cortical destruction. Hand location often favors benign diagnoses, but an aggressive appearance and cancer history override a casual assumption that every phalangeal lucency is an enchondroma.
prompt: What diagnosis should remain visible in an older patient with a destructive finger lesion and lung cancer?
answer: Metastasis, even though the hand is an uncommon site compared with the axial skeleton and proximal long bones.

title: A soft tissue mass belongs in the cortical assessment
body: The chondrosarcoma of a phalanx and distal femoral osteosarcoma on slide 36 illustrate extra-osseous components with cortical destruction. Tumor can also spread through cortical channels, so a large mass need not be accompanied by proportionally obvious radiographic cortical loss. Describe the soft tissues and request appropriate staging/extent imaging rather than focusing only on the intramedullary component.
prompt: What should you actively seek around an aggressive bone lesion?
answer: An extra-osseous component and subtle cortical permeation or breakthrough, with MRI when needed to define extent.

title: Run a mimic check before biopsy
body: The exhibit groups mimics as normal variants, developmental abnormalities, infection, metabolic/depositional disease, arthritis, trauma/iatrogenic lesions, and sclerosing dysplasias. These include humeral or calcaneal pseudocysts, cortical desmoid, Brodie abscess, brown tumor, infarction, gout, geodes, stress fracture, particle disease, myositis ossificans, biceps tenodesis, and melorheostosis. Use a plausible mechanism and characteristic location rather than attaching a mimic label to an unexplained aggressive finding.
prompt: What clinical history can prevent a mistaken tumor diagnosis?
answer: Prior trauma, surgery, repetitive loading, arthropathy, crystal deposition, infection, or a known dysplasia, matched to the imaging.
overlap: Visual application of a repeated principle: Recognize when the best answer is a mimic.

title: Intact trabeculae through a humeral lucency favor a pseudocyst
body: The proximal humeral pseudocyst on slide 38 lies in the greater tuberosity and retains normal trabeculae through the apparent lucency. CT confirms a normal anatomic variant. It can mimic myeloma, metastasis, or an epiphyseal tumor, but recognition of the expected site and retained architecture can prevent unnecessary biopsy.
prompt: What reassuring internal feature is visible through the humeral pseudocyst?
answer: Intact traversing bony trabeculae in the expected location.
overlap: Visual application of a repeated principle: Greater-tuberosity pseudocyst is not a true mass.

title: A prominent deltoid insertion can simulate a cortical lesion
body: Pseudotumor deltoideus on slide 38 is an anatomic variant at the lateral humeral deltoid insertion. Its characteristic insertional site and defined borders provide the key context. Compare the variant with the hydroxyapatite-deposition case on slide 42, which also involves the deltoid region but has a calcific deposit and secondary osseous involvement.
prompt: What location makes pseudotumor deltoideus recognizable?
answer: The lateral humeral cortex at the deltoid tendon insertion.

title: A femoral-neck herniation pit is a location-based mimic
body: The incidental femoral-neck lucency on slide 39 has a sharply sclerotic rim and represents a synovial herniation pit. Mechanical forces and an association with femoroacetabular impingement are discussed. The appearance can overlap osteoid osteoma, an intraosseous ganglion, Brodie abscess, or other lucencies, so precise site and symptoms remain important.
prompt: What mechanism and association are discussed for the femoral-neck pit?
answer: Mechanical forces, with an association described for femoroacetabular impingement.

title: Posteromedial distal femoral irregularity can be a cortical desmoid
body: Slide 39 shows a posterior medial distal femoral cortical irregularity in a young patient. This benign self-limiting entity is also called distal femoral cortical irregularity or a Bufkin lesion. Recognize the characteristic site and appearance to avoid mistaking insertional change for osteosarcoma or infection.
prompt: What site should make cortical desmoid a leading consideration?
answer: The posteromedial cortex of the distal femur, especially in a young patient.
overlap: Visual application of a repeated principle: Distal femoral cortical irregularity is a traction phenomenon.

title: A Brodie abscess can be nonsclerotic and aggressive
body: The calcaneal Brodie abscess on slide 40 has an ill-defined geographic margin rather than the classic sclerotic rim. MRI shows a relatively T1-bright lining around the cavity, the penumbra sign, and peripheral enhancement with surrounding edema. The sign supports subacute infection in context but should not be treated as an absolute exclusion of tumor.
prompt: What MRI clue supports Brodie abscess, and what is its limit?
answer: A T1-brighter cavity lining, the penumbra sign, supports infection; it does not replace the full assessment or necessary tissue/microbiologic diagnosis.
overlap: Visual application of a repeated principle: Brodie abscess is a physeal-adjacent mimic in the young.

title: Tophi plus periarticular erosion can resemble an aggressive mass
body: The severe foot case on slide 41 combines juxta-articular soft tissue nodules with extensive erosions and cortical destruction involving multiple joints and bones. Clinical gout, the periarticular distribution, and preserved overall mineralization help organize the diagnosis. A mass with bone erosion is not automatically a sarcoma when the pattern is centered on crystal arthropathy.
prompt: What ties the destructive foot lesions to gout rather than a single primary bone tumor?
answer: Tophi, a multi-joint periarticular erosive distribution, and the clinical history.

title: Prior imaging can reveal an extraosseous calcific deposit before bone invasion
body: The patient with breast cancer on slide 42 has a deltoid-region calcific focus with cortical involvement and intraosseous extension, initially concerning for metastasis. An earlier chest radiograph shows the same deposit at the insertion without cortical involvement, supporting hydroxyapatite deposition. Comparison imaging changes the mechanism from a primary destructive bone lesion to a calcific tendon-related process.
prompt: Which comparison resolves the misleading cancer-history case?
answer: An older radiograph demonstrates the calcific deposit at the deltoid insertion before cortical involvement developed.

title: Patchy periarticular osteopenia after injury can mimic infiltration
body: The ankle/foot case on slide 43 follows a talar fracture and shows diffuse patchy osteopenia across multiple adjacent bones, soft tissue symptoms, and preserved joint spaces. Disproportionate pain, hyperalgesia, edema, and skin/vascular changes support complex regional pain syndrome. Radiographs may initially be normal, so imaging alone neither establishes nor excludes the clinical syndrome.
prompt: What distribution and history favor CRPS over a focal bone tumor?
answer: Regional periarticular osteopenia involving several bones after injury, with disproportionate pain and autonomic or trophic changes.

title: Find the fracture line within a florid periosteal response
body: Slide 44 illustrates metatarsal stress fractures and a bisphosphonate-associated proximal femoral diaphyseal stress injury. Fatigue injury reflects excessive loading of normal bone; insufficiency injury reflects ordinary loading of abnormal bone. Early radiographs can be negative, while later fracture lines, resorption, and callus can resemble tumor or infection. MRI can clarify a radiographically occult stress injury.
prompt: What differentiates fatigue from insufficiency stress injury?
answer: Excessive load on normal bone versus normal load on weakened bone.

title: Dripping-candle-wax hyperostosis suggests melorheostosis
body: Slide 45 shows irregular flowing cortical hyperostosis in phalanges and along the fibula. The characteristic waxlike pattern and involvement of contiguous bones along a sclerotomal distribution distinguish this dysplasia from a focal surface tumor. The appendicular skeleton is more often involved than the axial skeleton.
prompt: Which pattern is the key visual discriminator?
answer: Irregular flowing cortical hyperostosis resembling dripping candle wax.

title: Medial clavicular hyperostosis belongs in a systemic pattern
body: In slide 46, medial clavicular and manubriosternal osteitis/hyperostosis occur in SAPHO syndrome, linking synovitis, acne, pustulosis, hyperostosis, and osteitis. The exhibit also mentions spinal, sacroiliac, and long-bone disease. In children, chronic recurrent multifocal osteomyelitis is an important inflammatory mimic. Ask about distribution and associated clinical findings rather than calling an isolated dense clavicle a tumor.
prompt: Which chest-wall locations are emphasized in SAPHO?
answer: The sternoclavicular region and adjacent anterior chest-wall articulations, including the manubriosternal joint.

title: The actual ACR report template is reproduced here
body:
Slides 47-48 reproduce the ACR radiography report template with permission. Begin with examination/views, date, clinical indication, technique, comparisons, demographic age group, and known malignancy. The template then separates lesion description from point values. It provides the exact report content that is referenced but not included in the supplied ACR article PDF.

ACR connection: Author-created checklist based on the article: indication and pertinent cancer history; comparison; lesion number, exact bone, longitudinal and transverse location, and size; density and matrix; margins, periosteal response, erosion, fracture, and extra-osseous mass; a concise differential; six-domain point total and Bone-RADS category if adequately characterized; and a clear next step. The paper mentions an e-only report template, but that appendix is absent from the supplied 17-page PDF, so this checklist is not presented as its exact template.
prompt: Where in the supplied source set can you see the actual ACR report template?
answer: RSNA slides 47-48.
overlap: This principle appears in both the textbook/exhibit and the ACR paper; reviewed together here.

title: The template records size and impending fracture separately from points
body: The findings template records three dimensions, size relative to bone diameter, exact bone, longitudinal and transverse location, density, matrix, margins, periosteal response, scalloping, fracture, and extra-osseous mass. It also has an impending-fracture field without a separate point value. The scoring column lists the six risk domains and a total. This separation prevents lesion size or impending fracture from being mistaken for an extra weighted domain.
prompt: Is impending fracture a seventh point-scoring domain in the reproduced template?
answer: No. It is separately documented for management; the weighted fracture domain refers to a pathological fracture.

title: Case: a 34-year-old with a distal femoral epiphyseal-metaphyseal lucency
body: The slide-50 case shows a central distal femoral lucency reaching the epiphysis, with no matrix, an IB margin, mild scalloping/remodeling, and no aggressive reaction, fracture, or mass. The rendered slide gives the final diagnosis as giant cell tumor. Its stated score is 3 points from the margin alone, category 2. Symptoms and local aggressiveness can still justify treatment-oriented referral.
prompt: Which features support GCT over a routine metaphyseal NOF in this case?
answer: Adult age, extension into the epiphysis, lack of matrix, and a nonsclerotic geographic margin.

title: Case: lung cancer with a destructive proximal humeral lesion
body: The 65-year-old man on slide 51 has an eccentric metaphyseal lucency, ill-defined geographic margin, Codman triangle, cortical destruction, and mass, with impending-fracture concern. The final diagnosis is lung-cancer metastasis. The slide sums 5 margin + 4 periosteal + 4 mass + 2 cancer-history points = 15, category 4. Its cortical-destruction row has no erosion points, so the displayed total should be identified as the source score rather than a definitive recalculation.
prompt: What are the immediate case-management concerns beyond naming metastasis?
answer: High malignancy concern, soft tissue extent, and mechanical/impending-fracture risk, requiring coordinated oncology/orthopedic evaluation.

title: Case: an older patient with chondroid matrix and a growing shoulder mass
body: The 80-year-old woman on slide 52 has a proximal humeral lesion with chondroid matrix, nongeographic destruction, Codman reaction, cortical loss, extra-osseous mass, and evidence of prior curettage/cement. The diagnosis is chondrosarcoma. The slide states 7 + 4 + 1 + 4 = 16, category 4. It labels moderate scalloping despite cortical destruction, an internal scoring discrepancy that does not alter the high-risk category.
prompt: What distinguishes this cartilage lesion from a bland enchondroma?
answer: Destructive margins, cortical breakthrough, an extra-osseous mass, and aggressive periosteal response.

title: Case: an osteoid osteoma receives an intermediate source score
body: The 15-year-old girl on slide 53 has a small distal radial cortical lucency/nidus with surrounding sclerosis and thickening. The exhibit diagnoses osteoid osteoma and assigns IB margin 3 plus solid reaction 2 = 5, category 3. This is the exhibit specific scoring, not a rule that every osteoid osteoma is category 3. The ACR article separately describes classic osteoid osteoma among very-low-risk examples. Use CT when nidus confirmation or treatment planning is needed.
prompt: Why should you avoid memorizing osteoid osteoma as a fixed category 3 diagnosis?
answer: Risk scoring depends on the assigned imaging features; the exhibit and ACR classic example illustrate different feature interpretations.

title: Case: osteoid matrix and a mass in an adolescent femoral lesion
body: The 18-year-old man on slide 54 has a distal femoral destructive lesion with osteoid mineralization, Codman reaction, cortical disruption, and extra-osseous mass. The diagnosis is osteosarcoma. The source states 7 margin + 4 periosteal + 4 mass = 15, category 4, while assigning 0 in the cortical row despite disruption. The high-risk conclusion remains supported; explain the inconsistency instead of turning that row into a scoring rule.
prompt: Which feature helps favor osteosarcoma within the aggressive adolescent differential?
answer: Osteoid matrix, combined with the destructive lesion and extra-osseous component.

title: Case: nonmineralized aggressive femoral lesion with fracture
body: The 24-year-old man on slide 55 has permeative/moth-eaten proximal femoral destruction, no matrix, multilamellated reaction, a mass, and a pathological fracture. The exhibit diagnoses Ewing sarcoma and totals 7 + 4 + 2 fracture + 4 mass = 17, category 4. The cortical-disruption row again receives 0 rather than a deep-erosion value, so preserve the source total with that qualification.
prompt: What follow-up issues should accompany the Ewing diagnosis?
answer: Fracture-related mechanical risk, local extent, staging, and coordinated biopsy/treatment planning.

title: Case: ground glass does not cancel deep cortical scalloping
body: The 71-year-old man on slide 56 has an expansile radial lesion with ground-glass density, cortical thinning, and deep scalloping. The diagnosis is fibrous dysplasia; the source assigns IB margin 3 plus deep erosion 2 = 5, category 3. It illustrates why a benign family name or recognizable matrix does not remove the need to assess the specific lesion and its mechanical consequences.
prompt: Which two features account for the intermediate score in the fibrous-dysplasia example?
answer: The assigned IB margin and deep endosteal scalloping.

title: Case: a scalloped NOF can remain very low risk
body: The 13-year-old boy on slide 57 has an eccentric distal femoral lucency with a sclerotic border and open physes. Moderate scalloping adds 1 to an IA margin worth 1: total 2, category 1. The final diagnosis is NOF. The source notes that many regress spontaneously, but a large lesion may fracture and symptomatic cases need clinical correlation.
prompt: How does this NOF reach two points while staying category 1?
answer: IA margin 1 plus moderate scalloping 1 totals 2, within the very-low-risk range.
